This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions; see the `README.md`
for more information.

- Defines a domain-specific language (DSL) for describing x64 instructions.

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.133.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/latest

`cranelift-assembler-x64-meta`

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and *could* be migrated there (though not
necessarily).

### Structure

- `dsl.rs`
- `instructions.rs`
- `generate.rs`

### Use

This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:

```
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
### Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

---

# cranelift_srcgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-srcgen/^0.133.1/

## Expand description

A source code generator.

This crate contains generic helper routines and classes for generating source code.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Defines an `Error`returned during source code generation.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fmtln](https://docs.rs/macro.fmtln.html)
- A macro that simplifies the usage of the `Formatter`
- [loc](https://docs.rs/macro.loc.html)
- A macro for constructing a `FileLocation`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileLocation.html)- Location
- Record a source location; preferably, use `loc`
- [Formatter](https://docs.rs/struct.Formatter.html)
- Collect source code to be written to a file and keep track of indentation.
- [Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)
- Match formatting class.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# krishiv_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-runtime/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_runtime/

## Expand description

Runtime traits and local backends for Krishiv.

Embedded mode runs batch SQL through the session `SqlEngine` (in `krishiv-api`).
Streaming plans are accepted here and executed via [ local_streaming](https://docs.rs/local_streaming/index.html) on
single-node backends (ADR-12.5).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [continuous_](https://docs.rs/continuous_stream/index.html)- stream
- Shared continuous streaming job state between session and in-process executor.
- [execution_](https://docs.rs/execution_runtime/index.html)- runtime
- Unified execution runtime across Embedded (in-process), SingleNode (local daemon), and Distributed modes.
- [flight_](https://docs.rs/flight_action/index.html)- action
- Typed Arrow Flight `DoAction`payloads for the Krishiv streaming control plane (B3, D2).
- [flight_](https://docs.rs/flight_client/index.html)- client
- Arrow Flight SQL client for `super::DistributedBackend`
- [flight_](https://docs.rs/flight_protocol/index.html)- protocol
- Krishiv Flight SQL comment protocol for catalog sync and remote streaming control.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/in_process/index.html)- process
- In-process coordinator + executor over shared mpsc/inbox transport (ADR-12.4).
- [in_](https://docs.rs/in_process_cluster/index.html)- process_ - cluster
- Session-scoped in-process coordinator + executor cluster (ADR-12.4 / ADR-13.3).
- [ivm_job](https://docs.rs/ivm_job/index.html)
- IVM job backends for remote and embedded modes.
- [local_](https://docs.rs/local_streaming/index.html)- streaming
- Bounded window execution (delegates to unified `krishiv-dataflow`operator runtime).
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/stream_kafka/index.html)- kafka
- Encode in-memory `RecordBatch``stream-kafka:`input partition descriptors.
- [streaming_](https://docs.rs/streaming_job/index.html)- job
- Ergonomic streaming job handle for the remote (coordinator HTTP) mode.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Distributed](https://docs.rs/struct.DistributedBackend.html)- Backend
- Distributed backend that routes plan execution to a remote coordinator via Arrow Flight SQL (GAP-RT-01 / ADR-12.3).
- [Embedded](https://docs.rs/struct.EmbeddedBackend.html)- Backend
- Embedded in-process backend: batch via session `SqlEngine`, streaming delegated to`SingleNodeBackend`
- [Execution](https://docs.rs/struct.ExecutionReport.html)- Report
- Minimal execution report for bootstrap backends.
- [IvmJob](https://docs.rs/struct.IvmJobRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry of IVM jobs hosted on this coordinator process.
- [JobId](https://docs.rs/struct.JobId.html)
- Typed job id identifier.
- [JobStatus](https://docs.rs/struct.JobStatus.html)
- Minimal job status surfaced by `krishiv jobs`.
- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.LocalJobRegistry.html)- JobRegistry
- Local in-memory job registry for bootstrap CLI/status behavior.
- [Remote](https://docs.rs/struct.RemoteStepSummary.html)- Step - Summary
- Summary returned by `execute_coordinator_ivm_step`
- [Single](https://docs.rs/struct.SingleNodeBackend.html)- Node - Backend
- Single-node in-process backend: accepts batch and streaming plans for local execution.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [IvmJob](https://docs.rs/enum.IvmJob.html)
- A coordinator-hosted IVM job: a single flow, or one auto-partitioned by key.
- [JobState](https://docs.rs/enum.JobState.html)
- Minimal job state for R1 local job listing.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/enum.RuntimeError.html)- Error
- Runtime errors shared by bootstrap backends and traits.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Execution](https://docs.rs/trait.ExecutionBackend.html)- Backend
- Runtime backend contract shared by embedded, single-node, and distributed modes.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_coordinator_batch_sql.html)- coordinator_ - batch_ - sql

- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_coordinator_ivm_restore.html)- coordinator_ - ivm_ - restore

- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_coordinator_ivm_restore_delta.html)- coordinator_ - ivm_ - restore_ - delta

- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_coordinator_ivm_snapshot.html)- coordinator_ - ivm_ - snapshot

- Run one IVM tick on a remote job. Returns a `RemoteStepSummary`

- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_coordinator_list_jobs.html)- coordinator_ - list_ - jobs
- List all jobs currently tracked by the coordinator (`GET /api/v1/jobs`).
- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_coordinator_physical_plan.html)- coordinator_ - physical_ - plan
- Execute a physical plan on the coordinator via HTTP (batch SQL or continuous register).
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_streaming_plan.html)- streaming_ - plan
- Returns true when the plan must run through the single-node streaming runtime rather than DataFusion batch execution.
- [streaming_](https://docs.rs/fn.streaming_spec_from_plan.html)- spec_ - from_ - plan

# sim_lib_lang_ruby - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-lang-ruby/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_lang_ruby/

## Expand description

Ruby DSL surface profile for the SIM runtime.

The kernel defines the codec, eval-policy, and `Expr` contracts; this crate
is a loadable language profile presenting a Ruby surface syntax over the
shared `Expr` graph, not a standalone interpreter.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ruby](https://docs.rs/struct.RubyBlockScope.html)- Block - Scope
- A labeled Ruby block scope targeted by `break`and`next`exits.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_ruby_dsl_profile.html)- ruby_ - dsl_ - profile
- Installs the Ruby DSL profile and its organ claims into a registry.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_blocks_fidelity_symbol.html)- blocks_ - fidelity_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby full-blocks fidelity badge (limited support).
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_break.html)- break
- Performs a Ruby `break`, escaping the block scope with`value`.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_conformance_test_symbol.html)- conformance_ - test_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby DSL control conformance test.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_control_fidelity_symbol.html)- control_ - fidelity_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby control-blocks fidelity badge.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dispatch_fidelity_symbol.html)- dispatch_ - fidelity_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby method-dispatch fidelity badge.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_matrix_row.html)- dsl_ - matrix_ - row
- Builds the Ruby DSL matrix row.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_profile.html)- dsl_ - profile
- Builds the `LanguageProfile`
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_dsl_source_cases.html)- dsl_ - source_ - cases
- Minimal source cases for the Ruby DSL matrix row.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_lowering_symbol.html)- lowering_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the Ruby lowering from surface forms to `Expr`.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_next.html)- next
- Performs a Ruby `next`, advancing the block scope with`value`.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_profile_symbol.html)- profile_ - symbol
- Stable symbol identifying the Ruby DSL language profile.
- [ruby_](https://docs.rs/fn.ruby_reader_symbol.html)- reader_ - symbol
- Stable symbol for the reader codec the Ruby surface decodes through.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_ruby_dsl_conformance_case.html)- ruby_ - dsl_ - conformance_ - case
- Runs one Ruby DSL source conformance case.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_ruby_dsl_matrix_row.html)- ruby_ - dsl_ - matrix_ - row
- Runs the Ruby DSL matrix row and publishes claim-backed cells.

# krishiv_ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-ui/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_ui/

## Expand description

R2 status API and server-rendered Web UI.

This crate exposes scheduler snapshots as a small Rust-native operations surface. It intentionally depends on the in-process R2 scheduler model rather than introducing Kubernetes clients or a separate frontend build.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [UiState](https://docs.rs/struct.UiState.html)
- Shared state for the R2 status server.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [UiError](https://docs.rs/enum.UiError.html)
- UI construction and handler errors.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [demo_](https://docs.rs/fn.demo_state.html)- state
- Create a deterministic demo state for local UI development and tests.
- [embedded_](https://docs.rs/fn.embedded_router.html)- router
- Build the UI-specific routes (jobs, executors, SQL editor, health dashboard) for embedding inside the coordinator HTTP server.
- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_state.html)- state
- Create an empty active coordinator state for real status serving.
- [router](https://docs.rs/fn.router.html)
- Build the R2 UI router.
- [router_](https://docs.rs/fn.router_with_token.html)- with_ - token
- Build the R2 UI router with an explicit auth token. When `Some`, the same routes as`router()`get wrapped in the bearer-token middleware. When`None`, the router behaves identically to a`KRISHIV_UI_TOKEN`-unset build.
- [serve](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html)
- Serve the R2 status API and Web UI with an existing listener.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [UiResult](https://docs.rs/type.UiResult.html)
- Shared UI result alias.

# plakat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/plakat/1.22.0/plakat/

## Expand description

plakat — local text-to-image, style transfer, LoRA, upscale, and color-key CLI built on candle.

This crate is primarily consumed as the `plakat` binary defined in
`src/main.rs`. The library target exists so examples (under
`examples/`) and integration tests (under `tests/`) can reach into
the same module surface the binary uses, without duplicating
non-trivial code like CLIP-H preprocessing or model loading.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [artefacts](https://docs.rs/artefacts/index.html)
- Artefact compositing — place named PNG cutouts into named zones of a generated image.
- [capability](https://docs.rs/capability/index.html)
- `plakat doctor --capability`— which supported models can run on the detected hardware, at a glance.
- [civitai](https://docs.rs/civitai/index.html)
- v0.16 phase 7: Civitai browser + downloader.
- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- [compile](https://docs.rs/compile/index.html)
- `plakat compile`— turn a prose- `prompts.txt`into a- `scenario`HJSON.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- [device](https://docs.rs/device/index.html)
- [error_](https://docs.rs/error_hints/index.html)- hints
- v0.33 phase 1: actionable error hints.
- [hf](https://docs.rs/hf/index.html)
- [hw](https://docs.rs/hw/index.html)
- Hardware probe for `plakat doctor --capability`.
- [imaging](https://docs.rs/imaging/index.html)
- [instance_](https://docs.rs/instance_guard/index.html)- guard
- Single-instance guard — refuse to start a second heavy plakat run on the
same host. On unified-memory machines (Apple Silicon) two concurrent
model/training runs share the SAME memory pool and thrash each other into
swap (or trip the `crate::memwatch`
- [llm](https://docs.rs/llm/index.html)
- Local LLM-based prompt enhancer. Runs a small quantized
instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct by default,
SmolLM2-360M-Instruct as a CPU-budget fallback) in-process via
candle’s `quantized_qwen2`/`quantized_llama`backends, so users get the v0.13 “enhance my prompt” workflow without an API key.
- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- `plakat map`— scale-aware procedural fantasy maps. MAP-1 ships the spec + the LLM geographic parser; the geometry engine (MAP-2+) and the renderer (MAP-3/linework, MAP-6/tiled-SD) follow. See- `Documentation/RFC_MAP_COMPILE_PLAN.md`.
- [memwatch](https://docs.rs/memwatch/index.html)
- Memory watchdog — graceful self-abort before a unified-memory host crash.
- [pipelines](https://docs.rs/pipelines/index.html)
- [preset](https://docs.rs/preset/index.html)
- v0.25: art-style presets — `--look`(medium axis) +`--genre`(subject-domain axis).
- [prompt](https://docs.rs/prompt/index.html)
- [scripting](https://docs.rs/scripting/index.html)
- v0.21: Bund scripting language integration.
- [style](https://docs.rs/style/index.html)
- Art-style detection and transfer.
- [ui](https://docs.rs/ui/index.html)

# krishiv_sql - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-sql/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_sql/

## Expand description

SQL planning and local execution seam for Krishiv.

This crate owns the DataFusion integration for R1 while keeping DataFusion
out of the long-term public API exposed by `krishiv-api`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use cep_sql::`- [MatchRecognizeStatement](https://docs.rs/cep_sql/struct.MatchRecognizeStatement.html);
- `pub use cep_sql::`- [execute_streaming_match_recognize](https://docs.rs/cep_sql/fn.execute_streaming_match_recognize.html);
- `pub use cep_sql::`- [parse_match_recognize](https://docs.rs/cep_sql/fn.parse_match_recognize.html);
- `pub use lakehouse::`- [AsOfTableRef](https://docs.rs/lakehouse/struct.AsOfTableRef.html);
- `pub use lakehouse::`- [MergeResult](https://docs.rs/lakehouse/struct.MergeResult.html);
- `pub use lakehouse::`- [MergeTargetUnsupportedError](https://docs.rs/lakehouse/struct.MergeTargetUnsupportedError.html);
- `pub use lakehouse::`- [preprocess_as_of_sql](https://docs.rs/lakehouse/fn.preprocess_as_of_sql.html);
- `pub use grammar::`- [FeatureEntry](https://docs.rs/grammar/struct.FeatureEntry.html);
- `pub use grammar::`- [FeatureStatus](https://docs.rs/grammar/enum.FeatureStatus.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [analyze](https://docs.rs/analyze/index.html)
- ANALYZE TABLE — collect column statistics from a batch.
- [catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)
- Catalog abstractions for Krishiv.
- [cep_sql](https://docs.rs/cep_sql/index.html)
- `MATCH_RECOGNIZE`SQL extension planning and execution (R16 S2).
- [connector_](https://docs.rs/connector_table/index.html)- table
- DataFusion `TableProviderFactory`implementations backed by`krishiv_connectors::ConnectorRegistry`
- [create_](https://docs.rs/create_function_ddl/index.html)- function_ - ddl
- Pre-processor for `CREATE FUNCTION … RETURNS TABLE`DDL.
- [grammar](https://docs.rs/grammar/index.html)
- SQL grammar and feature matrix for Krishiv.
- [incremental_](https://docs.rs/incremental_view/index.html)- view
- `CREATE INCREMENTAL VIEW`and- `DECLARE RECURSIVE VIEW`SQL extensions.
- [introspection_](https://docs.rs/introspection_sql/index.html)- sql
- `DESCRIBE`,- `SHOW COLUMNS`, and- `EXPLAIN`SQL intercepts.
- [kafka_](https://docs.rs/kafka_table/index.html)- table
- [lakehouse](https://docs.rs/lakehouse/index.html)
- R18 lakehouse SQL extensions: delta/hudi providers, AS OF, MERGE INTO.
- [live_](https://docs.rs/live_table/index.html)- table
- `CREATE LIVE TABLE`SQL extensions (R14 S1.1).
- [pipeline_](https://docs.rs/pipeline_ddl/index.html)- ddl
- Declarative pipeline DDL: `CREATE SOURCE`/`CREATE SINK`/`START PIPELINE`.
- [pivot_](https://docs.rs/pivot_sql/index.html)- sql
- E5.4 — PIVOT / UNPIVOT SQL macro rewrite layer.
- [recursive_](https://docs.rs/recursive_cte/index.html)- cte
- E5.3 — Recursive CTE: iterative fixpoint execution.
- [spark_](https://docs.rs/spark_sql_ext/index.html)- sql_ - ext
- Spark SQL extensions: LATERAL VIEW, TABLESAMPLE, TRANSFORM, DESCRIBE EXTENDED, etc. Spark SQL feature extensions — pre-processors for SQL constructs that DataFusion doesn’t parse natively.
- [sqlstate](https://docs.rs/sqlstate/index.html)
- SQLSTATE code mapping for Krishiv SQL errors.
- [streaming](https://docs.rs/streaming/index.html)
- [streaming_](https://docs.rs/streaming_tvf/index.html)- tvf
- Streaming window table-valued functions: TUMBLE, HOP, SESSION.
- [streaming_](https://docs.rs/streaming_window_plan/index.html)- window_ - plan
- Compile a windowed streaming SQL query into a `WindowExecutionSpec`
- [subquery](https://docs.rs/subquery/index.html)
- E5.1 — Correlated subquery decorrelation: EXISTS/IN/scalar subquery analysis.
- [unnest_](https://docs.rs/unnest_sql/index.html)- sql
- E5.2 — LATERAL / UNNEST SQL pre-processing.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [batch_](https://docs.rs/fn.batch_size_from_env.html)- size_ - from_ - env
- Resolve the batch size from `KRISHIV_BATCH_SIZE`env var.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_parallelism_from_env.html)- parallelism_ - from_ - env
- Resolve the default parallelism from `KRISHIV_TARGET_PARALLELISM`env var.
- [explain_](https://docs.rs/fn.explain_sql.html)- sql
- Create bootstrap `EXPLAIN`text for a SQL query.
- [explain_](https://docs.rs/fn.explain_sql_optimized.html)- sql_ - optimized
- Explain a SQL query including optimizer rule decisions.
- [explain_](https://docs.rs/fn.explain_sql_with_cost.html)- sql_ - with_ - cost
- Explain a SQL query and append a cost estimate from the provided cost model.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_public_expression.html)- public_ - expression
- Parse the stable SQL-expression subset into the same engine-owned AST used by Rust and Python.
- [plan_](https://docs.rs/fn.plan_sql.html)- sql
- Create a Krishiv logical plan wrapper for a SQL query without executing it.
- [pretty_](https://docs.rs/fn.pretty_batches.html)- batches
- Format Arrow batches for CLI and tests.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/fn.query_memory_limit_from_env.html)- memory_ - limit_ - from_ - env
- Resolve the default per-engine memory limit from the
`KRISHIV_QUERY_MEMORY_LIMIT_BYTES`environment variable.
- [referenced_](https://docs.rs/fn.referenced_table_names.html)- table_ - names
- Return all base table/relation names referenced by `query`.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_query_memory_limit_bytes.html)- query_ - memory_ - limit_ - bytes
- Resolve a per-engine DataFusion memory limit from a raw env var value.
`None`, unparseable, and zero values all mean “no limit” (the engine runs with DataFusion’s default unbounded pool).
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_streaming_match_recognize_limit.html)- streaming_ - match_ - recognize_ - limit
- Resolve the streaming MATCH_RECOGNIZE row cap from a raw env var value.
`None`and unparseable values fall back to the documented default of 100_000. Zero is rejected because it would mean “scan zero rows”.
- [streaming_](https://docs.rs/fn.streaming_match_recognize_limit_from_env.html)- match_ - recognize_ - limit_ - from_ - env
- Resolve the streaming MATCH_RECOGNIZE row cap from the
`KRISHIV_MATCH_RECOGNIZE_STREAMING_LIMIT`environment variable.

# modulino - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/modulino/0.3.0/modulino/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#modulino)Modulino

A hardware-agnostic, `no_std` Rust driver for Arduino Modulino breakout boards.

This crate provides drivers for the following Modulino devices:

- `Buttons`
- `Buzzer`
- `Pixels`
- `Distance`
- `Movement`
- `Knob`
- `Thermo`- `hs3003`
- `Joystick`
- `LatchRelay`
- `Vibro`
- `LedMatrix`
- `Pressure`
- `Light`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use modulino::{Pixels, Color};
// Create a Pixels instance with your I2C bus
let mut pixels = Pixels::new(i2c)?;
// Set the first LED to red
pixels.set_color(0, Color::RED, 50)?;
// Apply the changes
pixels.show()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `defmt`: Enable- `defmt`debug formatting for error types

[§](https://docs.rs#hardware-requirements)Hardware Requirements

All Modulino devices communicate over I2C at 100kHz. They use the Qwiic/STEMMA QT connector standard for easy daisy-chaining.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [addresses](https://docs.rs/addresses/index.html)
- Default I2C addresses for Modulino devices.
- [pinstrap](https://docs.rs/pinstrap/index.html)
- Pinstrap address map for device type detection.

# krishiv_state - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-state/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_state/

## Expand description

Public facade for `krishiv-state`.

Keyed state API with RocksDB backend for both ephemeral (tests/dev) and durable (file-backed) state storage.

State must be accessed only within `process_batch` or
`flush_triggered_windows` on the executor operator loop — never from
timer callbacks.

# yatrosci_bio_seq - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yatrosci-bio-seq/0.1.0/yatrosci_bio_seq/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#scirs-biological-sequences-advanced)SciRS Biological Sequences (Advanced)

Formal sequence analysis and bioinformatics. No simplified algorithms.

This crate provides:

- Pairwise Alignment (Smith-Waterman, Needleman-Wunsch)
- Substitution Matrices (BLOSUM62, PAM250)
- Statistical Bioinformatics (Hidden Markov Models foundations)
- Information Theory (Shannon Entropy of sequences)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [alignment](https://docs.rs/alignment/index.html)
- Sequence Alignment Algorithms
- [informatics](https://docs.rs/informatics/index.html)
- Statistics and Information Theory
- [sequence](https://docs.rs/sequence/index.html)
- Biological sequence data structures and transformations.
- [substitution](https://docs.rs/substitution/index.html)
- Substitution Models

# mongreldb_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mongreldb-core/0.20.1/mongreldb_core/

## Expand description

MongrelDB core — a log-structured columnar store with sub-ms writes, learned indexes over a shared row-id space, page-level native encryption, an MVCC-tagged content-addressed cache, and an AI-native access layer.

The crate owns the WAL + memtable + Bε-tree write path, sorted-run container formats, MVCC snapshots, page cache, encryption, compaction, and indexes.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [be_tree](https://docs.rs/be_tree/index.html)
- Buffered Bε-tree (B-epsilon-tree) over composite `(RowId, Epoch)`keys — the Phase 1 memtable target.
- [cache](https://docs.rs/cache/index.html)
- MVCC-tagged, content-addressed page cache.
- [catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)
- DB-wide catalog checkpoint (spec §5.1).
- [columnar](https://docs.rs/columnar/index.html)
- Plain columnar encode/decode for the prototype type set.
- [compaction](https://docs.rs/compaction/index.html)
- Tiered compaction (Phase 5) with snapshot retention.
- [constraint](https://docs.rs/constraint/index.html)
- Engine-side declarative constraints (unique, foreign key, check) enforced
authoritatively inside the core transaction path. Opt-in per-table via
`crate::schema::Schema::constraints``TableConstraints`
- [cursor](https://docs.rs/cursor/index.html)
- Lazy, page-aware native-column cursor for streaming scans (Phase 6.2).
- [database](https://docs.rs/database/index.html)
- Multi-table `Database`container (spec §5, §6, §10).
- [encryption](https://docs.rs/encryption/index.html)
- Native page-level encryption (optional, behind the `encryption`feature).
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- The engine tying the write and read paths together.
- [epoch](https://docs.rs/epoch/index.html)
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- [gc](https://docs.rs/gc/index.html)
- Operational tools: garbage collection and integrity check.
- [global_](https://docs.rs/global_idx/index.html)- idx
- Global index file — `_idx/global.idx`.
- [index](https://docs.rs/index/index.html)
- Indexes. All share the `crate::rowid::RowId`
- [manifest](https://docs.rs/manifest/index.html)
- Manifest — the atomic pointer to the current set of sorted runs.
- [memtable](https://docs.rs/memtable/index.html)
- In-memory write buffer (the “memtable”).
- [mutable_](https://docs.rs/mutable_run/index.html)- run
- Mutable run tier — the LSM layer between the skip-list memtable and the
immutable `.sr`sorted runs (Phase 11.1).
- [page](https://docs.rs/page/index.html)
- [pma](https://docs.rs/pma/index.html)
- Packed Memory Array — a cache-oblivious sorted array with amortized
`O(log² n)`insert and**no full rewrite per insert**.
- [query](https://docs.rs/query/index.html)
- Tool-call-native query surface.
- [reservoir](https://docs.rs/reservoir/index.html)
- Reservoir sampling for approximate analytics (Phase 8.2).
- [retention](https://docs.rs/retention/index.html)
- Global snapshot-retention registry for a multi-table `Database`.
- [rowid](https://docs.rs/rowid/index.html)
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- [sorted_](https://docs.rs/sorted_run/index.html)- run
- Sorted Run — the immutable columnar unit (`.sr`).
- [trace](https://docs.rs/trace/index.html)
- Query path instrumentation (OPTIMIZATIONS.md Priority 0 / 16).
- [tsv](https://docs.rs/tsv/index.html)
- TSV import/export (MongrelDB-compatible format).
- [txn](https://docs.rs/txn/index.html)
- Cross-table transactions on the shared WAL (spec §8.2, single-applier subset — parallelism arrives in P3).
- [wal](https://docs.rs/wal/index.html)
- Append-only, group-commit, torn-write-safe WAL.

# bpfix 0.1.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bpfix/0.1.5

# BPFix: making eBPF verifier errors more friendly

**BPFix makes eBPF verifier errors feel closer to Rust compiler errors.**

The Linux eBPF verifier is powerful, but its failure logs are hard to read. BPFix is a userspace diagnostic tool for that problem. It reads verifier logs from your existing workflow and turns them into source-level explanations that point to where the verifier lost the required proof.

## Quick Start

Install `bpfix` and load the prebuilt verifier failure:

```
 |
```
The command loads a real verifier failure from `bpfix-empirical`
(`stackoverflow-53136145`). The source parses either IPv4 or IPv6, derives a
UDP header pointer on each branch, checks the UDP header against `data_end`, and
then reads the destination port:

```
if   else if   else
if
    udph = ipv4_hdr + sizeof;
else
    udph = ipv6_hdr + sizeof;
if
    return 1;
dst_port = ;
```
That source shape is normal BPF C: the developer made the packet proof explicit.
The failure is in the verifier-visible proof lifecycle. One replay path reaches
the shared `udph->dest` load with `r5` as a scalar instead of a packet pointer:

```
from 31 to 34: ... R5_w=40 ...
; if (udph + sizeof(struct udphdr) > data_end) @ prog.c:267
34: (bf) r3 = r5                      ; R3_w=40 R5_w=40
35: (07) r3 += 8                      ; R3=48
36: (2d) if r3 > r2 goto pc+4         ; R2=pkt_end() R3=48
; dst_port = __constant_ntohs(((struct udphdr *)udph)->dest); @ prog.c:270
37: (69) r2 = *(u16 *)(r5 +2)
R5 invalid mem access 'scalar'
```
```
```
The raw log says where the verifier stopped, but not the source-level proof story. BPFix turns the trace into a Rust-style multi-span diagnostic:

```
error[BPFIX-E006]: verifier-visible compiler lowering hides the required proof
  = class: lowering_artifact
  = confidence: medium
  = diagnostic: supported, help: repair_hint, span: exact_pc
  = next action: provenance
  --> prog.c:270
   |
263 | if (ipv4_hdr)
    | ------------- nearby source context for pointer provenance
267 | if (udph + sizeof(struct udphdr) > data_end)
    | -------------------------------------------- verifier state changes from pkt to scalar before the rejected access
270 | dst_port = __constant_ntohs(((struct udphdr *)udph)->dest);
    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ rejected here: verifier sees a scalar where a pointer is required
   |
   = verifier[229]: R5 invalid mem access 'scalar'
   = note: nearest BPF instruction pc 37
   = note: parsed 60 verifier state snapshots
   = note[lowering]: compiler-lowered control flow hides an established packet-pointer proof
   = required proof: preserve a verifier-recognized pointer type at the operation that requires a pointer
help: Reacquire a verifier-tracked pointer before the rejected dereference.
help: Use the packet pointer that received the data_end proof, or rederive and recheck it before the load.
help: Keep the final access on a verifier-tracked pointer; rederive it from a checked base after scalar work.
```
This is the kind of failure that motivates the project: the program is not missing a generic "add a bounds check" hint. The useful answer is the proof lifecycle: where a verifier-recognized pointer proof exists, where branch-local provenance can be merged away, and where the rejected instruction finally needs that proof.

The example object is copied from
`bpfix-empirical/cases/stackoverflow-53136145/prog.o`; replace it with the
object you are debugging in your own project.

The CLI shape is intentionally small:

```
bpfix [OPTIONS] [LOG]
```
`LOG` can be a verifier, build, `bpftool`, libbpf, Aya, or BCC log. When `LOG`
is omitted or `-`, BPFix reads stdin. Positional input and stdin are always log
text. BPFix does not execute loader commands in the default path, and there is
no default command-execution workflow. Empirical corpus YAML and Docker-based execution
are explicit non-default modes; if Docker support is added, it should be selected
with an option such as `--docker`, not inferred from `LOG`. The output is always
plain text.

## Best Workflow

The best user experience is to keep your current BPF workflow and let BPFix explain the verifier log it already produces:

```
 |
```
or:

```
 |
```
with feature-gated object metadata, after installing with `--features object-analysis`:

```
```
BPFix does not need `case.yaml` for normal use. Empirical corpus YAML records are
evaluation fixtures; use the evaluation scripts when measuring the bundled
corpus.

The full user workflow is documented in `docs/user-guide.md`. More copyable
integration snippets live in `examples/`.

## Project Status

The maintained implementation is the Rust workspace:

```
crates/
  bpfix/        command-line diagnostic tool
  bpfanalysis/  verifier-log and BPF bytecode analysis primitives
```
The earlier Python version has been removed from the maintained tree. Python
scripts that remain under `bpfix-empirical/tools/` are empirical replay and corpus
maintenance helpers, not a second BPFix implementation and not part of the
public CLI.

The public CLI design lives in `docs/open-source-tool-design.md`, and the full
user workflow is in `docs/user-guide.md`. Evaluation methodology and
project planning notes live under `docs/evaluation/` and
`docs/project-status.md`; they are supporting material, not required reading for
normal use.

`bpfix-bench/` contains the frozen BPFix-Bench main75 LLM repair benchmark. It
is a source-first benchmark: a repair succeeds only when the candidate BPF C
file compiles, loads through the kernel verifier, and passes the case oracle.
Start with `bpfix-bench/README.md` for the benchmark contract and
`docs/evaluation/bpfix-bench-llm-repair-eval.md` for the reported raw-log versus
BPFix-diagnostic results.

The default `bpfix` CLI uses the verifier-log parser from `bpfanalysis`.
Object/CFG analysis is behind the `object-analysis` Cargo feature; that path
uses `libbpf-sys` and the `vendor/libbpf` submodule for BPF instruction and
program-type constants.

The current user-facing pipeline is log-first: `bpfix` parses verifier state
snapshots, instantiates the required verifier proof from the terminal error
and verifier state, extracts proof lifecycle events, and maps them back to
source comments when the log contains BTF/source annotations. Packet bounds,
scalar range, nullable pointer, stack readability, reference lifecycle, helper
capability, and pointer-provenance failures now produce parameterized proof
requirements instead of only terminal-error categories. When built with
`--features object-analysis`, the CLI accepts `--object prog.o`, builds
`ProgramCFG` summaries, and correlates verifier-state PCs with CFG sites when
the object section layout matches the loaded verifier program. Full BTF source
correlation is the next analysis layer, not a runtime requirement for the basic
CLI.

## What BPFix Handles

Current diagnostics focus on common verifier failures:

- packet bounds checks
- nullable map value pointers
- uninitialized stack reads
- reference lifetime leaks
- scalar range and variable-offset problems
- pointer type/provenance loss
- verifier-visible compiler lowering artifacts
- verifier precision limits and likely false positives
- verifier complexity and loop limits
- missing kernel/helper/program-type support
- dynptr lifetime and bounds issues

## Non-Goals

BPFix is not:

- a kernel patch
- a verifier replacement
- an automatic source-code repair tool
- a semantic correctness checker for accepted BPF programs

It explains why the verifier rejected a program and what proof the developer probably needs to make explicit.

## Development

Run tests:

```
```
Check the workspace:

```
```
Run the same lint gate used by CI:

```
```
Format code:

```
```
Run a smoke test:

```
```
Check release packaging:

```
```
This runs packaging checks, example consistency checks, the empirical corpus
`--reject-fallback` gate, and the feature-gated object-analysis CLI tests.

Release automation and the manual fallback are documented in
[docs/release.md](https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/bpfix/blob/master/docs/release.md).
`bpfix` depends on the sibling `bpfanalysis` crate; the publish workflow selects
the next unpublished patch version, publishes `bpfanalysis` first, waits for it
to appear in the crates.io index, and then publishes `bpfix`.

## Repository Layout

```
bpfix-empirical/       replayable verifier-failure corpus and raw examples
crates/bpfanalysis Rust analysis library
crates/bpfix       user-facing CLI
docs/project-status.md project planning and evaluation notes
docs/user-guide.md    install, getting logs, output, and CI usage
docs/open-source-tool-design.md public CLI contract
docs/release.md       release gates and crates.io publishing process
examples/          bpftool, libbpf, Aya, BCC, CI, and editor integration snippets
docs/evaluation/   evaluation and metric notes
bpfix-empirical/tools/ empirical replay and corpus-maintenance tools
vendor/libbpf/     libbpf submodule
```

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.133.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/0.133.1

`cranelift-assembler-x64-meta`

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and *could* be migrated there (though not
necessarily).

### Structure

- `dsl.rs`
- `instructions.rs`
- `generate.rs`

### Use

This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:

```
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
### Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

# cranelift_assembler_x64_meta::dsl - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/0.133.1/cranelift_assembler_x64_meta/dsl/index.html

## Expand description

Defines a domain-specific language (DSL) for describing x64 instructions.

This language is intended to be:

- compact–i.e., define an x64 instruction on a single line, and
- a close-to-direct mapping of what we read in the x64 reference manual.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use format::`- [Eflags](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Eflags.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Extension](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Extension.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Format](https://docs.rs/format/struct.Format.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Location](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Location.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Mutability](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Mutability.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Operand](https://docs.rs/format/struct.Operand.html);
- `pub use format::`- [OperandKind](https://docs.rs/format/enum.OperandKind.html);
- `pub use format::`- [RegClass](https://docs.rs/format/enum.RegClass.html);
- `pub use format::`- [align](https://docs.rs/format/fn.align.html);
- `pub use format::`- [fmt](https://docs.rs/format/fn.fmt.html);
- `pub use format::`- [implicit](https://docs.rs/format/fn.implicit.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- A DSL for describing x64 instruction formats–the shape of the operands.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Alternate](https://docs.rs/struct.Alternate.html)
- An alternate version of an instruction.
- [Custom](https://docs.rs/struct.Custom.html)
- [Evex](https://docs.rs/struct.Evex.html)

- An x64 instruction.

- Describe an instruction’s opcodes. From section 2.1.2 “Opcodes” in the reference manual:
- [Prefixes](https://docs.rs/struct.Prefixes.html)
- The allowed prefixes for an instruction. From the reference manual (section 2.1.1):
- [Rex](https://docs.rs/struct.Rex.html)
- The traditional x64 encoding.
- [Vex](https://docs.rs/struct.Vex.html)
- The VEX encoding, introduced for AVX instructions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- Enumerate the ways x64 encodes instructions.
- [Feature](https://docs.rs/enum.Feature.html)
- A CPU feature.
- [Features](https://docs.rs/enum.Features.html)
- A boolean term of CPU features.
- [Group1](https://docs.rs/enum.Group1Prefix.html)- Prefix
- [Group2](https://docs.rs/enum.Group2Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Contains the segment override prefixes or a (deprecated) branch hint when
used on a `Jcc`instruction. Note that using the segment override prefixes on a branch instruction is reserved. See section 2.1.1, “Instruction Prefixes,” in the reference manual.
- [Group3](https://docs.rs/enum.Group3Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Contains the operand-size override prefix (`0x66`); also used as a SIMD prefix. From the reference manual:
- [Group4](https://docs.rs/enum.Group4Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Contains the address-size override prefix (`0x67`). From the reference manual:
- [Length](https://docs.rs/enum.Length.html)
- Contains vector length definitions.
- [ModRm](https://docs.rs/enum.ModRmKind.html)- Kind
- [Opcode](https://docs.rs/enum.OpcodeMod.html)- Mod
- Indicate the size of the `reg`used when modifying the lower three bits of the opcode byte; this corresponds to the`+rb`,`+rw`,`+rd`, and`+ro`modifiers in the reference manual.
- [Tuple](https://docs.rs/enum.TupleType.html)- Type
- Tuple Type definitions used in EVEX encodings.
- [VexEscape](https://docs.rs/enum.VexEscape.html)
- Contains the escape sequences allowed for VEX-encoded instructions.
- [VexPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.VexPrefix.html)
- Contains the legacy prefixes allowed for VEX-encoded instructions.

- Generate the assembler `file`containing the core assembler logic; each of the DSL-defined instructions is emitted into a Rust`enum Inst`.

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.133.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

---

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.133.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/0.133.0

`cranelift-assembler-x64-meta`

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and *could* be migrated there (though not
necessarily).

### Structure

- `dsl.rs`
- `instructions.rs`
- `generate.rs`

### Use

This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:

```
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
### Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

---

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

---

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.128.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/0.128.3

`cranelift-assembler-x64-meta`

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and *could* be migrated there (though not
necessarily).

### Structure

- `dsl.rs`
- `instructions.rs`
- `generate.rs`

### Use

This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:

```
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
### Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

---

---

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.125.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/0.125.0

`cranelift-assembler-x64-meta`

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and *could* be migrated there (though not
necessarily).

### Structure

- `dsl.rs`
- `instructions.rs`
- `generate.rs`

### Use

This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:

```
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
### Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

---

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and *could* be migrated there (though not
necessarily).

### Structure

- `dsl.rs`
- `instructions.rs`
- `generate.rs`

### Use

This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:

```
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
### Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.

When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to disassemble this:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:

```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).

---

# cranelift-assembler-x64-meta 0.133.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/latest/source/README.md

```
This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions. It
is designed to fit in with Cranelift-specific logic (e.g., register allocation)
and only needs to define the x64 instructions Cranelift emits. It is written in
the style of `cranelift-codegen-meta` and _could_ be migrated there (though not
necessarily).
- --
This is primarily intended to be used for generating Rust code, i.e.,
`generate_rust_assembler("some-file.rs")`. It also has the ability to print
a list of the defined instructions:
```console
$ cargo run
andb: I(al, imm8) => 0x24 ib
andw: I(ax, imm16) => 0x25 iw
andl: I(eax, imm32) => 0x25 id
...
```
When something goes wrong, it can be helpful to compare the output of this
assembler with a known-good disassembler like XED.
When testing finds a miscompilation, it prints the emitted bytes. To use XED to
disassemble this:
```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -d 4080
```
To generate the expected bytes:
```
$ <path to xed>/obj/wkit/bin/xed -64 -A -e AND bpl IMM:48
```
XED also documents its CLI interface: [Intel XED command
interface](https://intelxed.github.io/ref-manual/group__CMDLINE.html).
```

---

# Match in cranelift_srcgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cranelift-srcgen/^0.133.1/struct.Match.html

`pub struct Match { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Match formatting class.

Match objects collect all the information needed to emit a Rust `match`
expression, automatically deduplicating overlapping identical arms.

Note that this class is ignorant of Rust types, and considers two fields with the same name to be equivalent. BTreeMap/BTreeSet are used to represent the arms in order to make the order deterministic.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# cranelift_assembler_x64_meta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/latest/target-redirect/cranelift_assembler_x64_meta/index.html

## Expand description

This crate generates Cranelift-specific assembly code for x64 instructions; see the `README.md`
for more information.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [dsl](https://docs.rs/dsl/index.html)
- Defines a domain-specific language (DSL) for describing x64 instructions.
- [instructions](https://docs.rs/instructions/index.html)
- Defines x64 instructions using the DSL.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_rust_assembler.html)- rust_ - assembler
- Generate the assembler `file`containing the core assembler logic; each of the DSL-defined instructions is emitted into a Rust`enum Inst`.

# cranelift_assembler_x64_meta::dsl - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cranelift-assembler-x64-meta/latest/target-redirect/cranelift_assembler_x64_meta/dsl/index.html

## Expand description

Defines a domain-specific language (DSL) for describing x64 instructions.

This language is intended to be:

- compact–i.e., define an x64 instruction on a single line, and
- a close-to-direct mapping of what we read in the x64 reference manual.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use format::`- [Eflags](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Eflags.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Extension](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Extension.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Format](https://docs.rs/format/struct.Format.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Location](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Location.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Mutability](https://docs.rs/format/enum.Mutability.html);
- `pub use format::`- [Operand](https://docs.rs/format/struct.Operand.html);
- `pub use format::`- [OperandKind](https://docs.rs/format/enum.OperandKind.html);
- `pub use format::`- [RegClass](https://docs.rs/format/enum.RegClass.html);
- `pub use format::`- [align](https://docs.rs/format/fn.align.html);
- `pub use format::`- [fmt](https://docs.rs/format/fn.fmt.html);
- `pub use format::`- [implicit](https://docs.rs/format/fn.implicit.html);
- `pub use format::`- [r](https://docs.rs/format/fn.r.html);
- `pub use format::`- [rw](https://docs.rs/format/fn.rw.html);
- `pub use format::`- [sxl](https://docs.rs/format/fn.sxl.html);
- `pub use format::`- [sxq](https://docs.rs/format/fn.sxq.html);
- `pub use format::`- [sxw](https://docs.rs/format/fn.sxw.html);
- `pub use format::`- [w](https://docs.rs/format/fn.w.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [format](https://docs.rs/format/index.html)
- A DSL for describing x64 instruction formats–the shape of the operands.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Alternate](https://docs.rs/struct.Alternate.html)
- An alternate version of an instruction.
- [Custom](https://docs.rs/struct.Custom.html)
- [Evex](https://docs.rs/struct.Evex.html)
- [Inst](https://docs.rs/struct.Inst.html)
- An x64 instruction.
- [Opcodes](https://docs.rs/struct.Opcodes.html)
- Describe an instruction’s opcodes. From section 2.1.2 “Opcodes” in the reference manual:
- [Prefixes](https://docs.rs/struct.Prefixes.html)
- The allowed prefixes for an instruction. From the reference manual (section 2.1.1):
- [Rex](https://docs.rs/struct.Rex.html)
- The traditional x64 encoding.
- [Vex](https://docs.rs/struct.Vex.html)
- The VEX encoding, introduced for AVX instructions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Customization](https://docs.rs/enum.Customization.html)
- [Encoding](https://docs.rs/enum.Encoding.html)
- Enumerate the ways x64 encodes instructions.
- [Feature](https://docs.rs/enum.Feature.html)
- A CPU feature.
- [Features](https://docs.rs/enum.Features.html)
- A boolean term of CPU features.
- [Group1](https://docs.rs/enum.Group1Prefix.html)- Prefix
- [Group2](https://docs.rs/enum.Group2Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Contains the segment override prefixes or a (deprecated) branch hint when
used on a `Jcc`instruction. Note that using the segment override prefixes on a branch instruction is reserved. See section 2.1.1, “Instruction Prefixes,” in the reference manual.
- [Group3](https://docs.rs/enum.Group3Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Contains the operand-size override prefix (`0x66`); also used as a SIMD prefix. From the reference manual:
- [Group4](https://docs.rs/enum.Group4Prefix.html)- Prefix
- Contains the address-size override prefix (`0x67`). From the reference manual:
- [Length](https://docs.rs/enum.Length.html)
- Contains vector length definitions.
- [ModRm](https://docs.rs/enum.ModRmKind.html)- Kind
- [Opcode](https://docs.rs/enum.OpcodeMod.html)- Mod
- Indicate the size of the `reg`used when modifying the lower three bits of the opcode byte; this corresponds to the`+rb`,`+rw`,`+rd`, and`+ro`modifiers in the reference manual.
- [Tuple](https://docs.rs/enum.TupleType.html)- Type
- Tuple Type definitions used in EVEX encodings.
- [VexEscape](https://docs.rs/enum.VexEscape.html)
- Contains the escape sequences allowed for VEX-encoded instructions.
- [VexPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.VexPrefix.html)
- Contains the legacy prefixes allowed for VEX-encoded instructions.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [ALL_](https://docs.rs/constant.ALL_FEATURES.html)- FEATURES
- List all CPU features.

# Function generate_rust_assembler

[Source](../src/cranelift_assembler_x64_meta/lib.rs.html#17-24) `pub fn generate_rust_assembler<P: `[AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)>>(dir: P, file: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [PathBuf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.PathBuf.html)

## Expand description

Generate the assembler `file` containing the core assembler logic; each of
the DSL-defined instructions is emitted into a Rust `enum Inst`.

[§](#panics)Panics

This function panics if we cannot update the file.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:
