# krishiv_engine_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-engine-core/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_engine_core/

## Expand description

Krishiv engine-core: the three-engine spine.

Krishiv runs **three distinct compute engines** that share one execution
contract:

- `EngineKind::Batch`
- `EngineKind::Incremental`
- `EngineKind::Streaming`

The **engine** (compute model), the **placement** (embedded / single-node /
distributed), and the **API surface** (SQL / Python / Rust) are three
independent axes. Every front-end compiles to a single [ CompiledJob](https://docs.rs/struct.CompiledJob.html); a

[runs it using placement-provided services carried by](https://docs.rs/trait.ComputeEngine.html)

`ComputeEngine`[. The same engine code therefore runs unchanged from an embedded in-process call to a distributed cluster — only the injected services differ.](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineRuntime.html)

`EngineRuntime`This crate is the bottom of the engine stack: it depends only on
`krishiv-common`, `krishiv-proto`, and Arrow, so every engine and front-end
crate can depend on it without a cycle.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use consolidate::`- [ConsolidatingSinkProvider](https://docs.rs/consolidate/struct.ConsolidatingSinkProvider.html);
- `pub use durable::`- [DurableCheckpointService](https://docs.rs/durable/struct.DurableCheckpointService.html);
- `pub use upsert::`- [UpsertSinkProvider](https://docs.rs/upsert/struct.UpsertSinkProvider.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [consolidate](https://docs.rs/consolidate/index.html)
- A retraction-aware sink wrapper that **consolidates**a changelog into its net materialized table before writing.
- [durable](https://docs.rs/durable/index.html)
- A file-backed `CheckpointService`
- [mem](https://docs.rs/mem/index.html)
- In-memory reference implementations of the runtime services.
- [upsert](https://docs.rs/upsert/index.html)
- A primary-key-keyed **upsert**sink wrapper: it*applies*a changelog by key before writing, rather than appending it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Changelog](https://docs.rs/struct.ChangelogBatch.html)- Batch
- A batch of rows tagged with per-row change kinds.
- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.CheckpointPayload.html)- Payload
- What one operator/task persists at one checkpoint epoch.
- [Compiled](https://docs.rs/struct.CompiledJob.html)- Job
- A fully compiled job — the single artifact produced by every front-end.
- [Engine](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineRuntime.html)- Runtime
- Placement-provided services handed to a `ComputeEngine`
- [JobHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.JobHandle.html)
- Handle to a running or completed job.
- [Sink](https://docs.rs/struct.SinkSpec.html)- Spec
- A sink that consumes one output relation/view of a job.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/struct.SourceSpec.html)- Spec
- A source of input batches for a job.
- [System](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemClock.html)- Clock
- Wall-clock implementation of `Clock`
- [Unknown](https://docs.rs/struct.UnknownEngine.html)- Engine
- Error returned when a string does not name a known engine.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Delivery](https://docs.rs/enum.DeliveryContract.html)- Contract
- The delivery guarantee requested for a job.
- [Engine](https://docs.rs/enum.EngineError.html)- Error
- Errors surfaced by the engine contract and its runtime services.
- [Engine](https://docs.rs/enum.EngineKind.html)- Kind
- Which of the three compute engines runs a job.
- [JobStatus](https://docs.rs/enum.JobStatus.html)
- Status of a submitted job.
- [Placement](https://docs.rs/enum.Placement.html)
- Where a job’s data-plane work runs.
- [RowKind](https://docs.rs/enum.RowKind.html)
- The kind of change a row represents in a changelog stream.
- [State](https://docs.rs/enum.StatePolicy.html)- Policy
- The state a job maintains, implied by its engine.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Checkpoint](https://docs.rs/trait.CheckpointService.html)- Service
- Coordinates durable checkpoints. Embedded persists locally; distributed routes through the scheduler’s checkpoint coordinator.
- [Clock](https://docs.rs/trait.Clock.html)
- Time source — wall clock in production, controllable in tests.

- Executes a job’s query off-engine — the placement seam for batch execution.
- [Shuffle](https://docs.rs/trait.ShuffleService.html)- Service
- Repartitions data across tasks. `None`in embedded placement (one task).
- [Sink](https://docs.rs/trait.SinkProvider.html)- Provider
- Opens writers for a job’s sinks.
- [Sink](https://docs.rs/trait.SinkWriter.html)- Writer
- Writes engine output. Batch writes insert-only batches; incremental and streaming write full changelogs.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/trait.SourceProvider.html)- Provider
- Opens readers for a job’s sources.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/trait.SourceReader.html)- Reader
- Reads input batches for one source.
- [State](https://docs.rs/trait.StateBackendFactory.html)- Backend - Factory
- Opens keyed-state backends for stateful engines.

- Decode Arrow IPC stream bytes produced by `encode_batch_ipc``RecordBatch`. Errors if the stream carries no batch or more than one.

# krishiv_delta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-delta/0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/krishiv_delta/

## Expand description

`krishiv-delta` — Incremental computing engine for Krishiv.

This crate implements the algebraic incremental view maintenance layer inspired by Feldera/DBSP (Z-set bilinear operators, Spine-style Trace) and CocoIndex (behavior versioning, convergent roll-forward commit, tiered change detection).

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

-
`DeltaBatch``RecordBatch`where each row has an`i64`weight:`+1`= insertion,`-1`= retraction,`0`= cancelled.
-
`Trace``DeltaBatch`es across ticks. Used by stateful operators (join, aggregate) to probe historical state efficiently.
-
`LogicFingerprint``(operator_uid, behavior_version)`. When bumped, it signals that an operator’s logic has changed and its cached Trace state should be discarded and recomputed.
-
`WatermarkTracker``max_ts - lateness_ms`are dropped; Trace entries below the watermark are eligible for GC.
-
`CoalescingMap`

[§](https://docs.rs#operator-library)Operator library

| Operator | Module | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| map / project | `operators::map` | Linear (no state) |
| filter | `operators::filter` | Linear (no state) |
| consolidate | `operators::consolidate` | Linear (no state) |
| join | `operators::join` | Bilinear (two Traces) |
| aggregate | `operators::aggregate` | Nonlinear (running state) |
| distinct | `operators::distinct` | Nonlinear (count map) |
| recursive | `operators::recursive` | Fixed-point loop |

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use behavior_version::`- [LogicFingerprint](https://docs.rs/behavior_version/struct.LogicFingerprint.html);
- `pub use behavior_version::`- [MemoKey](https://docs.rs/behavior_version/struct.MemoKey.html);
- `pub use coalesce::`- [CoalescingMap](https://docs.rs/coalesce/struct.CoalescingMap.html);
- `pub use delta_batch::`- [DeltaBatch](https://docs.rs/delta_batch/struct.DeltaBatch.html);

# atm_graft - Rust

## Expand description

Thin embedded ATM client crate for graft-aware host agents. Production nudge delivery uses one live advisory-stream receive loop when the selected transport supports same-host streaming.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [Noop](https://docs.rs/struct.NoopGraftObservability.html)- Graft - Observability
- No-op graft observability adapter.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionId.html)- Id
- Stable identifier for one active advisory session.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Graft](https://docs.rs/trait.GraftObservability.html)- Observability
- ATM-owned graft observability boundary supplied by the embedding host.
- [Host](https://docs.rs/trait.HostNudgeInjector.html)- Nudge - Injector
- Host-owned bridge for automatic between-tool-call nudge injection.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Session](https://docs.rs/type.SessionSnapshot.html)- Snapshot
- Public alias for the ATM-core graft session projection DTO.

# agent-team-mail 1.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/agent-team-mail/1.2.3

# agent-team-mail (`atm`)

`agent-team-mail` is the retained `1.0` CLI and core library for local ATM
mailbox workflows.

This repository is now the source of truth for publishing:

- `agent-team-mail`
- `agent-team-mail-core`

The installed command remains `atm`.

## What `1.0` Includes

The retained `1.0` release scope is the daemon-free CLI/core pair:

- `agent-team-mail`— the- `atm`CLI
- `agent-team-mail-core`— the core Rust library used by the CLI

This release line continues to consume the published `sc-observability` family
for retained logging and health reporting:

- `sc-observability`
- `sc-observability-types`
- `sc-observability-otlp`

This repo does not publish the retired legacy daemon, MCP, TUI, or CI-monitor
artifacts as part of the retained `1.0` surface.

## CLI Surface

## Configuration Notes

ATM resolves runtime identity and team context from the current CLI/config surface and uses the local Claude team directory layout for mailbox storage.

## Post-Send Hook

`atm send` can run an optional post-send hook configured in `.atm.toml`:

```
[[]]
 = "team-lead"
 = ["scripts/atm-nudge.sh", "team-lead"]
[[]]
 = "arch-ctm"
 = ["scripts/atm-nudge.sh", "arch-ctm"]
```
Behavior:

- Each `[[atm.post_send_hooks]]`rule binds one`recipient`and one`command`.
- `recipient`matches either one exact member name or- `*`for all recipients.
- Multiple matching rules all run, in config order.
- If `command[0]`is path-like, ATM resolves it relative to the directory containing`.atm.toml`.
- Bare executables like `bash`,`python3`, or`tmux`use normal`PATH`resolution.
- Recipient non-match is silent.
- ATM rejects retired `post_send_hook`,`post_send_hook_senders`,`post_send_hook_recipients`, and`post_send_hook_members`keys with migration guidance.
- ATM sets `ATM_POST_SEND`to a JSON payload with`{from, to, sender, recipient, team, message_id, requires_ack}`plus optional`task_id`when present.
- The hook gets 5 seconds to complete.
- Hook stderr is suppressed. Hook stdout may optionally return one JSON object with `level`,`message`, and optional`fields`for ATM to log.
- For troubleshooting hook diagnostics, combine `--stderr-logs`with`ATM_LOG=debug`to surface debug-level hook results on stderr.
- If the hook exits non-zero, fails to start, or times out, `atm send`still succeeds and prints a warning.

Example `ATM_POST_SEND` payload:

```
```
Example tmux auto-nudge hook for a Codex pane:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
recipient=""
team=""
```
Optional structured hook result on stdout:

```
```
Useful docs in this repo:

# krishiv-runtime

Unified runtime that wires together planning, scheduling, and execution.

## Overview

`krishiv-runtime` is the high-level orchestration layer:

- Connects SQL planning to scheduler and executor
- Manages session state and transaction lifecycle
- Handles Flight SQL protocol for client connections
- Coordinates embedded and distributed execution paths

## Features

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `kafka` | Kafka connector support |
| `vector-sinks` | Vector database sink support |

# arrow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrow/^58.3.0/

## Expand description

A complete, safe, native Rust implementation of [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org), a cross-language
development platform for in-memory data.

Please see the [arrow crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/arrow)
page for feature flags and tips to improve performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#columnar-format)Columnar Format

The [ array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html) module provides statically typed implementations of all the array types as defined
by the

[Arrow Columnar Format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html)

For example, an [ Int32Array](https://docs.rs/array/type.Int32Array.html) represents a nullable array of

`i32````
let array = Int32Array::from(vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)]);
assert_eq!(array.len(), 3);
assert_eq!(array.value(0), 1);
assert_eq!(array.is_null(1), true);
let collected: Vec<_> = array.iter().collect();
assert_eq!(collected, vec![Some(1), None, Some(3)]);
assert_eq!(array.values(), &[1, 0, 3])
```
It is also possible to write generic code for different concrete types. For example, since the following function is generic over all primitively typed arrays, when invoked the Rust compiler will generate specialized implementations with optimized code for each concrete type.

```
fn sum<T: ArrowPrimitiveType>(array: &PrimitiveArray<T>) -> T::Native
where
    T: ArrowPrimitiveType,
    T::Native: Sum
{
    array.iter().map(|v| v.unwrap_or_default()).sum()
}
assert_eq!(sum(&Float32Array::from(vec![1.1, 2.9, 3.])), 7.);
assert_eq!(sum(&TimestampNanosecondArray::from(vec![1, 2, 3])), 6);
```
And the following uses [ ArrayAccessor](https://docs.rs/array/trait.ArrayAccessor.html) to implement a generic function
over all arrays with comparable values.

```
fn min<T: ArrayAccessor>(array: T) -> Option<T::Item>
where
    T::Item: Ord
{
    ArrayIter::new(array).filter_map(|v| v).min()
}
assert_eq!(min(&Int32Array::from(vec![4, 2, 1, 6])), Some(1));
assert_eq!(min(&StringArray::from(vec!["b", "a", "c"])), Some("a"));
```
**For more examples, and details consult the  arrow_array docs.**

[§](https://docs.rs#type-erasure--trait-objects)Type Erasure / Trait Objects

It is common to write code that handles any type of array, without necessarily
knowing its concrete type. This is done using the [ Array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html) trait and using

[to determine the appropriate](https://docs.rs/datatypes/enum.DataType.html)

`DataType``downcast_ref`.```
fn impl_string(array: &StringArray) {}
fn impl_f32(array: &Float32Array) {}
fn impl_dyn(array: &dyn Array) {
    match array.data_type() {
        // downcast `dyn Array` to concrete `StringArray`
        DataType::Utf8 => impl_string(array.as_any().downcast_ref().unwrap()),
        // downcast `dyn Array` to concrete `Float32Array`
        DataType::Float32 => impl_f32(array.as_any().downcast_ref().unwrap()),
        _ => unimplemented!()
    }
}
```
You can use the [ AsArray](https://docs.rs/array/trait.AsArray.html) extension trait to facilitate downcasting:

```
fn impl_string(array: &StringArray) {}
fn impl_f32(array: &Float32Array) {}
fn impl_dyn(array: &dyn Array) {
    match array.data_type() {
        DataType::Utf8 => impl_string(array.as_string()),
        DataType::Float32 => impl_f32(array.as_primitive()),
        _ => unimplemented!()
    }
}
```
It is also common to want to write a function that returns one of a number of possible
array implementations. [ ArrayRef](https://docs.rs/array/type.ArrayRef.html) is a type-alias for

[which is frequently used for this purpose](https://docs.rs/array/trait.Array.html)

`Arc<dyn Array>````
fn parse_to_primitive<'a, T, I>(iter: I) -> PrimitiveArray<T>
where
    T: ArrowPrimitiveType,
    T::Native: FromStr,
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
    PrimitiveArray::from_iter(iter.into_iter().map(|val| T::Native::from_str(val).ok()))
}
fn parse_strings<'a, I>(iter: I, to_data_type: DataType) -> ArrayRef
where
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
   match to_data_type {
       DataType::Int32 => Arc::new(parse_to_primitive::<Int32Type, _>(iter)) as _,
       DataType::UInt32 => Arc::new(parse_to_primitive::<UInt32Type, _>(iter)) as _,
       _ => unimplemented!()
   }
}
let array = parse_strings(["1", "2", "3"], DataType::Int32);
let integers = array.as_any().downcast_ref::<Int32Array>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(integers.values(), &[1, 2, 3])
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compute-kernels)Compute Kernels

The [ compute](https://docs.rs/compute/index.html) module provides optimised implementations of many common operations,
for example the

`parse_strings` operation above could also be implemented as follows:```
fn parse_strings<'a, I>(iter: I, to_data_type: &DataType) -> Result<ArrayRef>
where
    I: IntoIterator<Item=&'a str>,
{
    let array = StringArray::from_iter(iter.into_iter().map(Some));
    arrow::compute::cast(&array, to_data_type)
}
let array = parse_strings(["1", "2", "3"], &DataType::UInt32).unwrap();
let integers = array.as_any().downcast_ref::<UInt32Array>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(integers.values(), &[1, 2, 3])
```
This module also implements many common vertical operations:

- All mathematical binary operators, such as `sub`
- All boolean binary operators such as `equality`
- `cast`
- `filter`
- `take`
- `sort`
- some string operators such as `substring``length`

```
let array = Int32Array::from_iter(0..100);
// Create a 32-bit integer scalar (single) value:
let scalar = Int32Array::new_scalar(60);
// find all rows in the array that are greater than 60
let predicate = gt(&array, &scalar).unwrap();
// copy all matching rows into a new array
let filtered = filter(&array, &predicate).unwrap();
let expected = Int32Array::from_iter(61..100);
assert_eq!(&expected, filtered.as_primitive::<Int32Type>());
```
As well as some horizontal operations, such as:

[§](https://docs.rs#tabular-representation)Tabular Representation

It is common to want to group one or more columns together into a tabular representation. This
is provided by [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) which combines a

[and a corresponding list of](https://docs.rs/datatypes/struct.Schema.html)

`Schema`[.](https://docs.rs/array/type.ArrayRef.html)

`ArrayRef````
let col_1 = Arc::new(Int32Array::from_iter([1, 2, 3])) as _;
let col_2 = Arc::new(Float32Array::from_iter([1., 6.3, 4.])) as _;
let batch = RecordBatch::try_from_iter([("col1", col_1), ("col_2", col_2)]).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-printing)Pretty Printing

See the [ util::pretty](https://docs.rs/util/pretty/index.html) module (requires the

`prettyprint` crate feature)[§](https://docs.rs#io)IO

This crate provides readers and writers for various formats to/from `RecordBatch`

Support for [Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/) is published as a [separate parquet crate](https://crates.io/crates/parquet)

Support for [Apache Avro](https://avro.apache.org/) is published as a [separate arrow-avro crate](https://crates.io/crates/arrow-avro)

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-compatibility)Serde Compatibility

[ arrow_json::reader::Decoder](https://docs.rs/arrow-json/58.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrow_json/reader/struct.Decoder.html) provides a mechanism to convert arbitrary, serde-compatible
structures into

[.](https://docs.rs/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`Whilst likely less performant than implementing a custom builder, as described in
[arrow_array::builder](https://docs.rs/array/builder/index.html), this provides a simple mechanism to get up and running quickly

```
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct MyStruct {
    int32: i32,
    string: String,
}
let schema = Schema::new(vec![
    Field::new("int32", DataType::Int32, false),
    Field::new("string", DataType::Utf8, false),
]);
let rows = vec![
    MyStruct{ int32: 5, string: "bar".to_string() },
    MyStruct{ int32: 8, string: "foo".to_string() },
];
let mut decoder = ReaderBuilder::new(Arc::new(schema)).build_decoder().unwrap();
decoder.serialize(&rows).unwrap();
let batch = decoder.flush().unwrap().unwrap();
// Expect batch containing two columns
let int32 = batch.column(0).as_primitive::<Int32Type>();
assert_eq!(int32.values(), &[5, 8]);
let string = batch.column(1).as_string::<i32>();
assert_eq!(string.value(0), "bar");
assert_eq!(string.value(1), "foo");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-topology)Crate Topology

The [ arrow](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs) project is implemented as multiple sub-crates, which are then re-exported by
this top-level crate.

Crate authors can choose to depend on this top-level crate, or just the sub-crates they need.

The current list of sub-crates is:

- `arrow-arith`
- `arrow-array`
- `arrow-buffer`
- `arrow-cast`
- `arrow-csv`
- `arrow-data`
- `arrow-ipc`
- `arrow-json`
- `arrow-ord`
- `arrow-row`
- `arrow-schema`
- `arrow-select`
- `arrow-string`

Some functionality is also distributed independently of this crate:

- `arrow-flight`- [Arrow Flight RPC](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Flight.html)
- `parquet`- [Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/)
- `arrow-avro`- [Apache Avro](https://avro.apache.org/)

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This project follows the [Apache Arrow Security Model](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/dev/format/Security.html).

Unexpected behavior (e.g., panics, crashes, or infinite loops) triggered by
malformed input is considered a **bug**, not a security vulnerability,
unless it is **exploitable** by an attacker to

- Execute arbitrary code (Remote Code Execution);
- Exfiltrate sensitive information from process memory (Information Disclosure);

If you think you have found a security vulnerability, please follow the
reporting instructions in the [security policy](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Like many crates, this crate makes use of `unsafe` where prudent. However, it endeavors to be
sound. Specifically, **it should not be possible to trigger undefined behavior using safe APIs.**

Undefined behavior using safe APIs is considered a bug, not a security
vulnerability, unless it can be exploited. Please see the [security policy](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for details.

For more information on the use of `unsafe`, see [here](https://github.com/apache/arrow-rs/tree/main/arrow#safety).

[§](https://docs.rs#higher-level-processing)Higher-level Processing

This crate aims to provide reusable, low-level primitives for operating on columnar data. For
more sophisticated query processing workloads, consider checking out [DataFusion](https://github.com/apache/arrow-datafusion). This
orchestrates the primitives exported by this crate into an embeddable query engine, with
SQL and DataFrame frontends, and heavily influences this crate’s roadmap.

# arrow_flight - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/arrow-flight/^58.3.0/

## Expand description

A native Rust implementation of [Apache Arrow Flight](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Flight.html)
for exchanging [Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org) data between processes.

Please see the [arrow-flight crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/arrow-flight)
page for feature flags and more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This crate contains:

-
Low level [prost](https://docs.rs/prost/0.14.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/prost/index.html)generated structs for Flight gRPC protobuf messages, such as`FlightData``FlightInfo``Location``Ticket`
-
Low level [tonic](https://docs.rs/tonic/0.14.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tonic/index.html)generated`flight_service_client``flight_service_server`
-
Support for [Flight SQL](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/FlightSql.html)in`sql``flight-sql`feature of this crate to be activated.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use client::`- [FlightClient](https://docs.rs/client/struct.FlightClient.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- Mid Level `FlightClient`
- [decode](https://docs.rs/decode/index.html)
- Decoder to create `RecordBatch``FlightData``FlightRecordBatchStream`

- Encoder to create `FlightData``RecordBatch``FlightDataEncoderBuilder`

- Common error types

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.Action.html)
- An opaque action specific for the service.
- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionType.html)- Type
- Describes an available action, including both the name used for execution along with a short description of the purpose of the action.
- [Basic](https://docs.rs/struct.BasicAuth.html)- Auth
- A message for doing simple auth.
- [Cancel](https://docs.rs/struct.CancelFlightInfoRequest.html)- Flight - Info - Request
- The request of the CancelFlightInfo action.
- [Cancel](https://docs.rs/struct.CancelFlightInfoResult.html)- Flight - Info - Result
- The result of the CancelFlightInfo action.
- [Criteria](https://docs.rs/struct.Criteria.html)
- A service specific expression that can be used to return a limited set of available Arrow Flight streams.
- [Empty](https://docs.rs/struct.Empty.html)
- [Flight](https://docs.rs/struct.FlightData.html)- Data
- A batch of Arrow data as part of a stream of batches.
- [Flight](https://docs.rs/struct.FlightDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- The name or tag for a Flight. May be used as a way to retrieve or generate a flight or be used to expose a set of previously defined flights.
- [Flight](https://docs.rs/struct.FlightEndpoint.html)- Endpoint
- A particular stream or split associated with a flight.
- [Flight](https://docs.rs/struct.FlightInfo.html)- Info
- The access coordinates for retrieval of a dataset. With a FlightInfo, a consumer is able to determine how to retrieve a dataset.
- [Handshake](https://docs.rs/struct.HandshakeRequest.html)- Request
- The request that a client provides to a server on handshake.
- [Handshake](https://docs.rs/struct.HandshakeResponse.html)- Response
- [IpcMessage](https://docs.rs/struct.IpcMessage.html)
- IpcMessage represents a `Schema`in the format expected in`FlightInfo.schema`
- [Location](https://docs.rs/struct.Location.html)
- A location where a Flight service will accept retrieval of a particular stream given a ticket.
- [Poll](https://docs.rs/struct.PollInfo.html)- Info
- The information to process a long-running query.
- [PutResult](https://docs.rs/struct.PutResult.html)
- [Renew](https://docs.rs/struct.RenewFlightEndpointRequest.html)- Flight - Endpoint - Request
- The request of the RenewFlightEndpoint action.
- [Result](https://docs.rs/struct.Result.html)
- An opaque result returned after executing an action.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaAsIpc.html)- AsIpc
- SchemaAsIpc represents a pairing of a `Schema`with IpcWriteOptions
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaResult.html)- Result
- Wrap the result of a getSchema call
- [Ticket](https://docs.rs/struct.Ticket.html)
- An opaque identifier that the service can use to retrieve a particular portion of a stream.

# base64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64/^0.22.1/

## Expand description

Correct, fast, and configurable [base64](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Base64) decoding and encoding. Base64
transports binary data efficiently in contexts where only plain text is
allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Use an [ Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html) to decode or encode base64, configured with the base64
alphabet and padding behavior best suited to your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#engine-setup)Engine setup

There is more than one way to encode a stream of bytes as “base64”.
Different applications use different encoding
[alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding behaviors](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-alphabet)Encoding alphabet

Almost all base64 [alphabets](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) use `A-Z`, `a-z`, and
`0-9`, which gives nearly 64 characters (26 + 26 + 10 = 62), but they differ
in their choice of their final 2.

Most applications use the [standard](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.STANDARD.html) alphabet specified
in [RFC 4648](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-4).  If that’s all you need, you can get started
quickly by using the pre-configured
[ STANDARD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.STANDARD.html) engine, which is also available
in the

[module as shown here, if you prefer a minimal](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use`
footprint.```
use base64::prelude::*;
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.decode(b"+uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(BASE64_STANDARD.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "/+wgVQA=");
```
Other common alphabets are available in the [ alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#url-safe-alphabet)URL-safe alphabet

The standard alphabet uses `+` and `/` as its two non-alphanumeric tokens,
which cannot be safely used in URL’s without encoding them as `%2B` and
`%2F`.

To avoid that, some applications use a [“URL-safe” alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/constant.URL_SAFE.html),
which uses `-` and `_` instead. To use that alternative alphabet, use the
[ URL_SAFE](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.URL_SAFE.html) engine. This example doesn’t
use

[to show what a more explicit](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)

`prelude``use` would look like.```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::URL_SAFE, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.decode(b"-uwgVQA=")?, b"\xFA\xEC\x20\x55\0");
assert_eq!(URL_SAFE.encode(b"\xFF\xEC\x20\x55\0"), "_-wgVQA=");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#padding-characters)Padding characters

Each base64 character represents 6 bits (2⁶ = 64) of the original binary data, and every 3 bytes of input binary data will encode to 4 base64 characters (8 bits × 3 = 6 bits × 4 = 24 bits).

When the input is not an even multiple of 3 bytes in length, [canonical](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4648#section-3.5)
base64 encoders insert padding characters at the end, so that the output
length is always a multiple of 4:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg==");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8=");
assert_eq!(STANDARD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
Canonical encoding ensures that base64 encodings will be exactly the same,
byte-for-byte, regardless of input length. But the `=` padding characters
aren’t necessary for decoding, and they may be omitted by using a
[ NO_PAD](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/constant.NO_PAD.html) configuration:

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD_NO_PAD, Engine as _};
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b""),    "");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"f"),   "Zg");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"fo"),  "Zm8");
assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.encode(b"foo"), "Zm9v");
```
The pre-configured `NO_PAD` engines will reject inputs containing padding
`=` characters. To encode without padding and still accept padding while
decoding, create an [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with
that [padding mode](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.DecodePaddingMode.html).

`assert_eq!(STANDARD_NO_PAD.decode(b"Zm8="), Err(base64::DecodeError::InvalidPadding));`[§](https://docs.rs#further-customization)Further customization

Decoding and encoding behavior can be customized by creating an
[engine](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurpose.html) with an [alphabet](https://docs.rs/alphabet/struct.Alphabet.html) and
[padding configuration](https://docs.rs/engine/general_purpose/struct.GeneralPurposeConfig.html):

```
use base64::{engine, alphabet, Engine as _};
// bizarro-world base64: +/ as the first symbols instead of the last
let alphabet =
    alphabet::Alphabet::new("+/ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789")
    .unwrap();
// a very weird config that encodes with padding but requires no padding when decoding...?
let crazy_config = engine::GeneralPurposeConfig::new()
    .with_decode_allow_trailing_bits(true)
    .with_encode_padding(true)
    .with_decode_padding_mode(engine::DecodePaddingMode::RequireNone);
let crazy_engine = engine::GeneralPurpose::new(&alphabet, crazy_config);
let encoded = crazy_engine.encode(b"abc 123");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#memory-allocation)Memory allocation

The [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and [encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) engine methods
allocate memory for their results – `decode` returns a `Vec<u8>` and
`encode` returns a `String`. To instead decode or encode into a buffer that
you allocated, use one of the alternative methods:

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding)Decoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::decode` | returns a new `Vec<u8>` | always |
| `Engine::decode_vec` | appends to provided `Vec<u8>` | if `Vec`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::decode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#encoding)Encoding

| Method | Output | Allocates memory |
|---|---|---|
| `Engine::encode` | returns a new `String` | always |
| `Engine::encode_string` | appends to provided `String` | if `String`lacks capacity |
| `Engine::encode_slice` | writes to provided `&[u8]` | never |

[§](https://docs.rs#input-and-output)Input and output

The `base64` crate can [decode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.decode) and
[encode](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html#method.encode) values in memory, or
[ DecoderReader](https://docs.rs/read/struct.DecoderReader.html) and

[provide streaming decoding and encoding for any](https://docs.rs/write/struct.EncoderWriter.html)

`EncoderWriter`[readable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)or

[writable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)byte stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#decoding-1)Decoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, read::DecoderReader};
let mut input = io::stdin();
let mut decoder = DecoderReader::new(&mut input, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut decoder, &mut io::stdout())?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#encoding-1)Encoding

```
use base64::{engine::general_purpose::STANDARD, write::EncoderWriter};
let mut output = io::stdout();
let mut encoder = EncoderWriter::new(&mut output, &STANDARD);
io::copy(&mut io::stdin(), &mut encoder)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#display)Display

If you only need a base64 representation for implementing the
[ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) trait, use

[:](https://docs.rs/display/struct.Base64Display.html)

`Base64Display````
use base64::{display::Base64Display, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};
let value = Base64Display::new(b"\0\x01\x02\x03", &STANDARD);
assert_eq!("base64: AAECAw==", format!("base64: {}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If length calculations result in overflowing `usize`, a panic will result.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- Deprecated
- Decode base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets using the specified [Engine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.Engine.html).
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Decode the input into the provided output slice.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_engine_vec.html)- engine_ - vec - Deprecated
- Decode from string reference as octets.
- [decoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.decoded_len_estimate.html)- len_ - estimate
- Returns a conservative estimate of the decoded size of `encoded_len`base64 symbols (rounded up to the next group of 3 decoded bytes).
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the `STANDARD`engine
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine.html)- engine - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 using the provided `Engine`into a new`String`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_slice.html)- engine_ - slice - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied slice.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_engine_string.html)- engine_ - string - Deprecated
- Encode arbitrary octets as base64 into a supplied `String`.
- [encoded_](https://docs.rs/fn.encoded_len.html)- len
- Calculate the base64 encoded length for a given input length, optionally including any appropriate padding bytes.

# datafusion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/datafusion/^53.1.0/

## Expand description

[DataFusion](https://datafusion.apache.org/) is an extensible query engine written in Rust that
uses [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org) as its in-memory format. DataFusion’s target users are
developers building fast and feature rich database and analytic systems,
customized to particular workloads. Please see the [DataFusion website](https://datafusion.apache.org) for
additional documentation, [use cases](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/introduction.html#use-cases) and examples.

“Out of the box,” DataFusion offers [SQL](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/index.html) and [ Dataframe](https://docs.rs/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html) APIs,
excellent

[performance](https://benchmark.clickhouse.com/), built-in support for CSV, Parquet, JSON, and Avro, extensive customization, and a great community.

[Python Bindings](https://github.com/apache/datafusion-python)are also available.

DataFusion features a full query planner, a columnar, streaming, multi-threaded,
vectorized execution engine, and partitioned data  sources. You can
customize DataFusion at almost all points including additional data sources,
query languages, functions, custom operators and more.
See the [Architecture](https://docs.rs#architecture) section below for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The main entry point for interacting with DataFusion is the
[ SessionContext](https://docs.rs/execution/context/struct.SessionContext.html).

[s represent expressions such as](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr``a + b`.[§](https://docs.rs#dataframe)DataFrame

To execute a query against data stored
in a CSV file using a [ DataFrame](https://docs.rs/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html):

```
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
// create the dataframe
let df = ctx
    .read_csv("tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
    .await?;
// create a plan
let df = df
    .filter(col("a").lt_eq(col("b")))?
    .aggregate(vec![col("a")], vec![min(col("b"))])?
    .limit(0, Some(100))?;
// execute the plan
let results: Vec<RecordBatch> = df.collect().await?;
// format the results
let pretty_results =
    arrow::util::pretty::pretty_format_batches(&results)?.to_string();
let expected = vec![
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| a | min(?table?.b) |",
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| 1 | 2              |",
    "+---+----------------+",
];
assert_eq!(pretty_results.trim().lines().collect::<Vec<_>>(), expected);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#sql)SQL

To execute a query against a CSV file using [SQL](https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/sql/index.html):

```
let ctx = SessionContext::new();
ctx.register_csv("example", "tests/data/example.csv", CsvReadOptions::new())
    .await?;
// create a plan
let df = ctx
    .sql("SELECT a, MIN(b) FROM example WHERE a <= b GROUP BY a LIMIT 100")
    .await?;
// execute the plan
let results: Vec<RecordBatch> = df.collect().await?;
// format the results
let pretty_results =
    arrow::util::pretty::pretty_format_batches(&results)?.to_string();
let expected = vec![
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| a | min(example.b) |",
    "+---+----------------+",
    "| 1 | 2              |",
    "+---+----------------+",
];
assert_eq!(pretty_results.trim().lines().collect::<Vec<_>>(), expected);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-examples)More Examples

There are many additional annotated examples of using DataFusion in the [datafusion-examples](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/tree/main/datafusion-examples) directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

You can find a formal description of DataFusion’s architecture in our
[SIGMOD 2024 Paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3626246.3653368).

[§](https://docs.rs#design-goals)Design Goals

DataFusion’s Architecture Goals are:

-
Work “out of the box”: Provide a very fast, world class query engine with minimal setup or required configuration.
-
Customizable everything: All behavior should be customizable by implementing traits.
-
Architecturally boring 🥱: Follow industrial best practice rather than trying cutting edge, but unproven, techniques.

With these principles, users start with a basic, high-performance engine and specialize it over time to suit their needs and available engineering capacity.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview--presentations)Overview  Presentations

The following presentations offer high level overviews of the different components and how they interact together.

- [Apr 2023]: The Apache DataFusion Architecture talks
- [July 2022]: DataFusion and Arrow: Supercharge Your Data Analytical Tool with a Rusty Query Engine: [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Rii1VTn3seQ)and[slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1q1bPibvu64k2b7LPi7Yyb0k3gA1BiUYiUbEklqW1Ckc/view#slide=id.g11054eeab4c_0_1165)
- [March 2021]: The DataFusion architecture is described in *Query Engine Design and the Rust-Based DataFusion in Apache Arrow*:[recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K6eCAVEk4kU)(DataFusion content starts[~ 15 minutes in](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K6eCAVEk4kU&t=875s)) and[slides](https://www.slideshare.net/influxdata/influxdb-iox-tech-talks-query-engine-design-and-the-rustbased-datafusion-in-apache-arrow-244161934)
- [February 2021]: How DataFusion is used within the Ballista Project is described in *Ballista: Distributed Compute with Rust and Apache Arrow*:[recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZZHQaOap9pQ)

[§](https://docs.rs#customization-and-extension)Customization and Extension

DataFusion is designed to be highly extensible, so you can
start with a working, full featured engine, and then
specialize any behavior for your use case. For example,
some projects may add custom [ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html) operators, or create their own
query language that directly creates

[rather than using the built in SQL planner,](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[.](https://docs.rs/sql/planner/struct.SqlToRel.html)

`SqlToRel`In order to achieve this, DataFusion supports extension at many points:

- read from any datasource (`TableProvider`
- define your own catalogs, schemas, and table lists (`catalog``CatalogProvider`
- build your own query language or plans (`LogicalPlanBuilder`
- declare and use user-defined functions (`ScalarUDF``AggregateUDF``WindowUDF`
- add custom plan rewrite passes (`AnalyzerRule``OptimizerRule``PhysicalOptimizerRule`
- extend the planner to use user-defined logical and physical nodes (`QueryPlanner`

You can find examples of each of them in the [datafusion-examples](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/tree/main/datafusion-examples) directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#query-planning-and-execution-overview)Query Planning and Execution Overview

[§](https://docs.rs#sql-1)SQL

```
                Parsed with            SqlToRel creates
                sqlparser              initial plan
┌───────────────┐           ┌─────────┐             ┌─────────────┐
│   SELECT *    │           │Query {  │             │Project      │
│   FROM ...    │──────────▶│..       │────────────▶│  TableScan  │
│               │           │}        │             │    ...      │
└───────────────┘           └─────────┘             └─────────────┘
  SQL String                 sqlparser               LogicalPlan
                             AST nodes
```
-
The query string is parsed to an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) `Statement`[sqlparser](https://docs.rs/sqlparser/latest/sqlparser).
-
The AST is converted to a `LogicalPlan``Expr``SqlToRel`

[§](https://docs.rs#dataframe-1)DataFrame

When executing plans using the [ DataFrame](https://docs.rs/dataframe/struct.DataFrame.html) API, the process is
identical as with SQL, except the DataFrame API builds the

[directly using](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[. Systems that have their own custom query languages typically also build](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/struct.LogicalPlanBuilder.html)

`LogicalPlanBuilder`[directly.](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[§](https://docs.rs#planning)Planning

```
            AnalyzerRules and      PhysicalPlanner          PhysicalOptimizerRules
            OptimizerRules         creates ExecutionPlan    improve performance
            rewrite plan
┌─────────────┐        ┌─────────────┐      ┌─────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────┐
│Project      │        │Project(x, y)│      │ProjectExec      │        │ProjectExec      │
│  TableScan  │──...──▶│  TableScan  │─────▶│  ...            │──...──▶│  ...            │
│    ...      │        │    ...      │      │   DataSourceExec│        │   DataSourceExec│
└─────────────┘        └─────────────┘      └─────────────────┘        └─────────────────┘
 LogicalPlan            LogicalPlan         ExecutionPlan             ExecutionPlan
```
To process large datasets with many rows as efficiently as possible, significant effort is spent planning and optimizing, in the following manner:

-
The `LogicalPlan``AnalyzerRule`
-
The `LogicalPlan``OptimizerRule`
-
The `LogicalPlan``ExecutionPlan``PhysicalPlanner`
-
The `ExecutionPlan``PhysicalOptimizerRule`

[§](https://docs.rs#data-sources)Data Sources

```
Planning       │
requests       │            TableProvider::scan
information    │            creates an
such as schema │            ExecutionPlan
               │
               ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌───────────────┐
  │                         │         │               │
  │impl TableProvider       │────────▶│DataSourceExec │
  │                         │         │               │
  └─────────────────────────┘         └───────────────┘
        TableProvider
        (built in or user provided)    ExecutionPlan
```
A [ TableProvider](https://docs.rs/datasource/trait.TableProvider.html) provides information for planning and
an

[for execution. DataFusion includes two built-in table providers that support common file formats and require no runtime services,](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[and](https://docs.rs/datasource/listing/struct.ListingTable.html)

`ListingTable`[. You can add support for any other data source and/or file formats by implementing the](https://docs.rs/datasource/struct.MemTable.html)

`MemTable`[trait.](https://docs.rs/datasource/trait.TableProvider.html)

`TableProvider`See also:

-
`ListingTable`
-
`MemTable``RecordBatch`
-
`StreamingTable`

[§](https://docs.rs#plan-representations)Plan Representations

[§](https://docs.rs#logical-plans)Logical Plans

Logical planning yields [ LogicalPlan](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html) nodes and

[representing expressions which are](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr`[aware and represent statements independent of how they are physically executed. A](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/datatypes/struct.Schema.html)

`Schema`[is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of other](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[s, each potentially containing embedded](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)

`LogicalPlan`[s.](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr`[ LogicalPlan](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html)s can be rewritten with

[API, see the](https://docs.rs/common/tree_node/trait.TreeNode.html)

`TreeNode`[for more details.](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/logical_plan/tree_node/index.html)

`tree_node module`[ Expr](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)s can also be rewritten with

[API and simplified using](https://docs.rs/common/tree_node/trait.TreeNode.html)

`TreeNode`[. Examples of working with and executing](https://docs.rs/optimizer/simplify_expressions/struct.ExprSimplifier.html)

`ExprSimplifier`[s can be found in the](https://docs.rs/prelude/enum.Expr.html)

`Expr`[example](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/main/datafusion-examples/examples/query_planning/expr_api.rs)

`expr_api`.rs[§](https://docs.rs#physical-plans)Physical Plans

An [ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html) (sometimes referred to as a “physical plan”)
is a plan that can be executed against data. It a DAG of other

[s each potentially containing expressions that implement the](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[trait.](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/trait.PhysicalExpr.html)

`PhysicalExpr`Compared to a [ LogicalPlan](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.LogicalPlan.html), an

[has additional concrete information about how to perform calculations (e.g. hash vs merge join), and how data flows during execution (e.g. partitioning and sortedness).](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[cp_solver](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/intervals/cp_solver/index.html) performs range propagation analysis on [ PhysicalExpr](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/trait.PhysicalExpr.html)s and

[can prove certain boolean](https://docs.rs/physical_optimizer/pruning/struct.PruningPredicate.html)

`PruningPredicate`[s used for filtering can never be](https://docs.rs/physical_expr/trait.PhysicalExpr.html)

`PhysicalExpr``true` using additional statistical information.[§](https://docs.rs#execution)Execution

```
           ExecutionPlan::execute             Calling next() on the
           produces a stream                  stream produces the data
┌────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────┐
│ProjectExec     │      │impl                     │    ┌───▶│RecordBatch │
│  ...           │─────▶│SendableRecordBatchStream│────┤    └────────────┘
│  DataSourceExec│      │                         │    │    ┌────────────┐
└────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────┘    ├───▶│RecordBatch │
              ▲                                        │    └────────────┘
ExecutionPlan │                                        │         ...
              │                                        │
              │                                        │    ┌────────────┐
            PhysicalOptimizerRules                     ├───▶│RecordBatch │
            request information                        │    └────────────┘
            such as partitioning                       │    ┌ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                                                       └───▶ None        │
                                                            └ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
```
[ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)s process data using the

[Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org)memory format, making heavy use of functions from the

[arrow](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/index.html)crate. Values are represented with

[, which are either](https://docs.rs/logical_expr/enum.ColumnarValue.html)

`ColumnarValue`[(single constant values) or](https://docs.rs/scalar/enum.ScalarValue.html)

`ScalarValue`[(Arrow Arrays).](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/type.ArrayRef.html)

`ArrayRef`Calling [ execute](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html#tymethod.execute) produces 1 or more partitions of data,
as a

[, which implements a pull based execution API. Calling](https://docs.rs/execution/type.SendableRecordBatchStream.html)

`SendableRecordBatchStream`

`next()``.await` will incrementally compute and return the next
[. Balanced parallelism is achieved using](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[Volcano style](https://doi.org/10.1145/93605.98720)“Exchange” operations implemented by

[.](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/repartition/struct.RepartitionExec.html)

`RepartitionExec`While some recent research such as [Morsel-Driven Parallelism](https://db.in.tum.de/~leis/papers/morsels.pdf) describes challenges
with the pull style Volcano execution model on NUMA architectures, in practice DataFusion achieves
similar scalability as systems that use push driven schedulers [such as DuckDB](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/1583).
See the [DataFusion paper in SIGMOD 2024](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/files/15149988/DataFusion_Query_Engine___SIGMOD_2024-FINAL-mk4.pdf) for more details.

See the [implementors of  ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html#implementors) for a list of physical operators available.

[§](https://docs.rs#streaming-execution)Streaming Execution

DataFusion is a “streaming” query engine which means [ ExecutionPlan](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)s incrementally
read from their input(s) and compute output one

[at a time by continually polling](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[s. Output and intermediate](https://docs.rs/execution/type.SendableRecordBatchStream.html)

`SendableRecordBatchStream`[s each have approximately](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch``batch_size` rows,
which amortizes per-batch overhead of execution.Note that certain operations, sometimes called “pipeline breakers”,
(for example full sorts or hash aggregations) are fundamentally non streaming and
must read their input fully before producing **any** output. As much as possible,
other operators read a single [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) from their input to produce a
single

[as output.](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`For example, given this SQL:

`SELECT name FROM 'data.parquet' WHERE id > 10`An simplified DataFusion execution plan is shown below. It first reads
data from the Parquet file, then applies the filter, then the projection,
and finally produces output. Each step processes one [ RecordBatch](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html) at a
time. Multiple batches are processed concurrently on different CPU cores
for plans with multiple partitions.

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────┐
│ Parquet     │───▶│ DataSource   │───▶│ FilterExec     │───▶│ ProjectionExec   │───▶│ Results  │
│ File        │    │              │    │                │    │                  │    │          │
└─────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────┘
                   (reads data)        (id > 10)             (keeps "name" col)
                   RecordBatch ───▶    RecordBatch ────▶     RecordBatch ────▶        RecordBatch
```
DataFusion uses the classic “pull” based control flow (explained more in the next section) to implement streaming execution. As an example, consider the following SQL query:

`SELECT date_trunc('month', time) FROM data WHERE id IN (10,20,30);`The diagram below shows the call sequence when a consumer calls [ next()](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.next) to
get the next

[of output. While it is possible that some steps run on different threads, typically tokio will use the same thread that called](https://docs.rs/common/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[to read from the input, apply the filter, and return the results without interleaving any other operations. This results in excellent cache locality as the same CPU core that produces the data often consumes it immediately as well.](https://docs.rs/futures-util/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_util/stream/stream/trait.StreamExt.html#method.next)

`next()````
Step 3: FilterExec calls next()       Step 2: ProjectionExec calls
        on input Stream                  next() on input Stream
        ┌ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─      ┌ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ┐
                           │                                               Step 1: Consumer
        ▼                        ▼                           │               calls next()
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓     ┏━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓      ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃                ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ◀ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
┃  DataSource    ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ┃
┃    (e.g.       ┃     ┃    FilterExec     ┃      ┃     ProjectionExec     ┃
┃ ParquetSource) ┃     ┃id IN (10, 20, 30) ┃      ┃date_bin('month', time) ┃
┃                ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ┣ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ▶
┃                ┃     ┃                   ┃      ┃                        ┃
┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛     ┗━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━┛      ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
        │                  ▲                                 ▲          Step 6: ProjectionExec
                           │     │                           │        computes date_trunc into a
        └ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─       ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─          new RecordBatch returned
             ┌─────────────────────┐                ┌─────────────┐          from client
             │     RecordBatch     │                │ RecordBatch │
             └─────────────────────┘                └─────────────┘
          Step 4: DataSource returns a        Step 5: FilterExec returns a new
               single RecordBatch            RecordBatch with only matching rows
```
DataFusion automatically runs each plan with multiple CPU cores using
a [Tokio](https://tokio.rs) [ Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html) as a thread pool. While tokio is most commonly used
for asynchronous network I/O, the combination of an efficient, work-stealing
scheduler, and first class compiler support for automatic continuation
generation (

`async`) also makes it a compelling choice for CPU intensive
applications as explained in the [Using Rustlang’s Async Tokio Runtime for CPU-Bound Tasks](https://thenewstack.io/using-rustlangs-async-tokio-runtime-for-cpu-bound-tasks/)blog.

The number of cores used is determined by the `target_partitions`
configuration setting, which defaults to the number of CPU cores.
While preparing for execution, DataFusion tries to create this many distinct
`async` [ Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html)s for each

[. The](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[s for certain](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[s, such as](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/trait.ExecutionPlan.html)

`ExecutionPlan`[and](https://docs.rs/datafusion/latest/datafusion/physical_plan/repartition/struct.RepartitionExec.html)

`RepartitionExec`[, spawn](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/coalesce_partitions/struct.CoalescePartitionsExec.html)

`CoalescePartitionsExec`[Tokio](https://tokio.rs)

[s, that run on threads managed by the](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/task/index.html)

`task`[. Many DataFusion](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)

`Runtime`[s perform CPU intensive processing.](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[§](https://docs.rs#cooperative-scheduling)Cooperative Scheduling

DataFusion uses cooperative scheduling, which means that each [ Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html)
is responsible for yielding control back to the

[after some amount of work is done. Please see the](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)

`Runtime`[module documentation for more details.](https://docs.rs/physical_plan/coop/index.html)

`coop`[§](https://docs.rs#network-io-and-cpu-intensive-tasks)Network I/O and CPU intensive tasks

Using `async` for CPU intensive tasks makes it easy for [ TableProvider](https://docs.rs/datasource/trait.TableProvider.html)s
to perform network I/O using standard Rust

`async` during execution.
However, this design also makes it very easy to mix CPU intensive and latency
sensitive I/O work on the same thread pool ([). Using the same (default)](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)

`Runtime`[is convenient, and often works well for initial development and processing local files, but it can lead to problems under load and/or when reading from network sources such as AWS S3.](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)

`Runtime`[§](https://docs.rs#optimizing-latency-throttled-cpu--io-under-highly-concurrent-load)Optimizing Latency: Throttled CPU / IO under Highly Concurrent Load

If your system does not fully utilize either the CPU or network bandwidth
during execution, or you see significantly higher tail (e.g. p99) latencies
responding to network requests, **it is likely you need to use a different
**. The

`Runtime` for DataFusion plans[thread_pools example](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/blob/main/datafusion-examples/examples/query_planning/thread_pools.rs)has an example of how to do so.

As shown below, using the same [ Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html) for both CPU intensive processing
and network requests can introduce significant delays in responding to
those network requests. Delays in processing network requests can and does
lead network flow control to throttle the available bandwidth in response.
This effect can be especially pronounced when running multiple queries
concurrently.

```
                                                                         Legend
                                                                         ┏━━━━━━┓
                           Processing network request                    ┃      ┃  CPU bound work
                           is delayed due to processing                  ┗━━━━━━┛
                           CPU bound work                                ┌─┐
                                                                         │ │       Network request
                                        ││                               └─┘       processing
                                        ││
                               ─ ─ ─ ─ ─  ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
                              │                                            │
                              ▼                                            ▼
┌─────────────┐           ┌─┐┌─┐┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓┌─┐
│             │thread 1   │ ││ │┃     Decoding      ┃┃     Filtering     ┃│ │
│             │           └─┘└─┘┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛└─┘
│             │           ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
│Tokio Runtime│thread 2   ┃   Decoding   ┃     Filtering     ┃   Decoding   ┃       ...
│(thread pool)│           ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
│             │     ...                               ...
│             │           ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓┌─┐ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
│             │thread N   ┃     Decoding      ┃     Filtering     ┃│ │ ┃   Decoding   ┃
└─────────────┘           ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛└─┘ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
                          ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶
                                                                                          time
```
The bottleneck resulting from network throttling can be avoided
by using separate [ Runtime](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/runtime/struct.Runtime.html)s for the different types of work, as shown
in the diagram below.

```
                   A separate thread pool processes network       Legend
                   requests, reducing the latency for
                   processing each request                        ┏━━━━━━┓
                                                                  ┃      ┃  CPU bound work
                                        │                         ┗━━━━━━┛
                                         │                        ┌─┐
                              ┌ ─ ─ ─ ─ ┘                         │ │       Network request
                                 ┌ ─ ─ ─ ┘                        └─┘       processing
                              │
                              ▼  ▼
┌─────────────┐           ┌─┐┌─┐┌─┐
│             │thread 1   │ ││ ││ │
│             │           └─┘└─┘└─┘
│Tokio Runtime│                                          ...
│(thread pool)│thread 2
│             │
│"IO Runtime" │     ...
│             │                                                   ┌─┐
│             │thread N                                           │ │
└─────────────┘                                                   └─┘
                          ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶
                                                                                          time
┌─────────────┐           ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
│             │thread 1   ┃     Decoding      ┃┃     Filtering     ┃
│             │           ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
│Tokio Runtime│           ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
│(thread pool)│thread 2   ┃   Decoding   ┃     Filtering     ┃   Decoding   ┃       ...
│             │           ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
│ CPU Runtime │     ...                               ...
│             │           ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
│             │thread N   ┃     Decoding      ┃     Filtering     ┃   Decoding   ┃
└─────────────┘           ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
                         ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶
                                                                                          time
```
Note that DataFusion does not use [ tokio::task::spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.50.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/task/blocking/fn.spawn_blocking.html) for
CPU-bounded work, because

`spawn_blocking` is designed for blocking **IO**, not designed CPU bound tasks. Among other challenges, spawned blocking tasks can’t yield waiting for input (can’t call

`await`) so they
can’t be used to limit the number of concurrent CPU bound tasks or
keep the processing pipeline to the same core.[§](https://docs.rs#state-management-and-configuration)State Management and Configuration

[ ConfigOptions](https://docs.rs/config/struct.ConfigOptions.html) contain options to control DataFusion’s
execution.

The state required to execute queries is managed by the following structures:

-
`SessionContext``LogicalPlan`
-
`TaskContext``MemoryPool``DiskManager``ObjectStoreRegistry`
-
`ExecutionProps`

[§](https://docs.rs#resource-management)Resource Management

The amount of memory and temporary local disk space used by
DataFusion when running a plan can be controlled using the
[ MemoryPool](https://docs.rs/execution/memory_pool/trait.MemoryPool.html) and

[. Other runtime options can be found on](https://docs.rs/execution/struct.DiskManager.html)

`DiskManager`[.](https://docs.rs/execution/runtime_env/struct.RuntimeEnv.html)

`RuntimeEnv`[§](https://docs.rs#crate-organization)Crate Organization

Most users interact with DataFusion via this crate (`datafusion`), which re-exports
all functionality needed to build and execute queries.

There are three other crates that provide additional functionality that must be used directly:

- `datafusion_proto`
- `datafusion_substrait`
- `datafusion_sqllogictest`

DataFusion is internally split into multiple sub crates to
enforce modularity and improve compilation times. See the
[list of modules](https://docs.rs#modules) for all available sub-crates. Major ones are

- [datafusion_common](https://docs.rs/datafusion-common/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_common/index.html): Common traits and types
- [datafusion_catalog](https://docs.rs/datafusion-catalog/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_catalog/index.html): Catalog APIs such as- `SchemaProvider`- `CatalogProvider`
- [datafusion_datasource](https://docs.rs/datafusion-datasource/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_datasource/index.html): File and Data IO such as- `FileSource`- `DataSink`
- [datafusion_session](https://docs.rs/datafusion-session/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_session/index.html):- `Session`
- [datafusion_execution](https://docs.rs/datafusion-execution/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_execution/index.html): State and structures needed for execution
- [datafusion_expr](https://docs.rs/datafusion-expr/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_expr/index.html):- `LogicalPlan`- `Expr`
- [datafusion_functions](https://docs.rs/datafusion-functions/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_functions/index.html): Scalar function packages
- [datafusion_functions_aggregate](https://docs.rs/datafusion-functions-aggregate/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_functions_aggregate/index.html): Aggregate functions such as- `MIN`,- `MAX`,- `SUM`, etc
- [datafusion_functions_nested](https://docs.rs/datafusion-functions-nested/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_functions_nested/index.html): Scalar function packages for- `ARRAY`s,- `MAP`s and- `STRUCT`s
- [datafusion_functions_table](https://docs.rs/datafusion-functions-table/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_functions_table/index.html): Table Functions such as- `GENERATE_SERIES`
- [datafusion_functions_window](https://docs.rs/datafusion-functions-window/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_functions_window/index.html): Window functions such as- `ROW_NUMBER`,- `RANK`, etc
- [datafusion_optimizer](https://docs.rs/datafusion-optimizer/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_optimizer/index.html):- `OptimizerRule`- `AnalyzerRule`
- [datafusion_physical_expr](https://docs.rs/datafusion-physical-expr/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_physical_expr/index.html):- `PhysicalExpr`
- [datafusion_physical_plan](https://docs.rs/datafusion-physical-plan/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_physical_plan/index.html):- `ExecutionPlan`
- [datafusion_physical_optimizer](https://docs.rs/datafusion-physical-optimizer/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_physical_optimizer/index.html):- `ExecutionPlan`
- [datafusion_sql](https://docs.rs/datafusion-sql/53.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/datafusion_sql/index.html): SQL planner (- `SqlToRel`

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# krishiv_ivm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-ivm/=0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/

## Expand description

Incremental View Maintenance (IVM) engine for Krishiv.

`IncrementalFlow` is the primary API: register views, feed source deltas,
call `step_datafusion()` each tick, and subscribe to output `DeltaBatch`es.

# krishiv_plan - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-plan/=0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/

## Expand description

Logical and physical plan types for Krishiv.

R1 bootstrap keeps these types deliberately small. Later R1 work will bridge them to DataFusion logical and physical plans without exposing DataFusion as the long-term public Krishiv API.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cep](https://docs.rs/cep/index.html)
- Complex event processing (CEP) sequential pattern matcher (R16 S2).
- [expression](https://docs.rs/expression/index.html)
- Versioned, engine-owned public expression and scalar type contract.
- [governance](https://docs.rs/governance/index.html)
- Minimal authentication and access-control interfaces for Krishiv.
- [optimizer](https://docs.rs/optimizer/index.html)
- Query optimizer traits and infrastructure for Krishiv.
- [task_](https://docs.rs/task_fragment/index.html)- fragment
- Typed task fragments with explicit execution kind (unified batch/streaming).
- [udf](https://docs.rs/udf/index.html)
- User-defined function (UDF) extension framework for Krishiv.
- [window](https://docs.rs/window/index.html)
- Streaming window plan configuration and fragment encoding (unified execution).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Logical](https://docs.rs/struct.LogicalPlan.html)- Plan
- Krishiv logical plan wrapper.
- [Physical](https://docs.rs/struct.PhysicalPlan.html)- Plan
- Krishiv physical plan wrapper.
- [Plan](https://docs.rs/struct.PlanDiff.html)- Diff
- Summary of structural differences between two physical plans.
- [Plan](https://docs.rs/struct.PlanNode.html)- Node
- A small bootstrap plan node used by both logical and physical plans.
- [Plan](https://docs.rs/struct.PlanSchema.html)- Schema
- Output schema for a plan node.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemaField.html)- Field
- One field in a plan schema.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Execution](https://docs.rs/enum.ExecutionKind.html)- Kind
- Whether a plan represents bounded batch work, unbounded streaming, or IVM.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldType.html)- Type
- Data type for a plan schema field.
- [Join](https://docs.rs/enum.JoinType.html)- Type
- Join variant used in `NodeOp::Join`.
- [NodeOp](https://docs.rs/enum.NodeOp.html)
- Typed operator classification for a plan node.
- [Partitioning](https://docs.rs/enum.Partitioning.html)
- Partitioning strategy for a plan node’s output.
- [Plan](https://docs.rs/enum.PlanError.html)- Error
- Errors returned by plan encoding, decoding, and validation operations.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_PLAN_NODES.html)- PLAN_ - NODES
- Maximum number of nodes allowed in a single plan.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_plans.html)- plans
- Compute the structural diff between two physical plans.
- [lower_](https://docs.rs/fn.lower_to_physical.html)- to_ - physical
- Validate and lower a logical plan into a physical plan.

# krishiv_sql - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/krishiv-sql/=0.1.0-nightly.202607030148/

## Expand description

SQL planning and local execution seam for Krishiv.

This crate owns the DataFusion integration for R1 while keeping DataFusion
out of the long-term public API exposed by `krishiv-api`.

- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_streaming_match_recognize_limit.html)- streaming_ - match_ - recognize_ - limit
- Resolve the streaming MATCH_RECOGNIZE row cap from a raw env var value.
`None`and unparseable values fall back to the documented default of 100_000. Zero is rejected because it would mean “scan zero rows”.
- [streaming_](https://docs.rs/fn.streaming_match_recognize_limit_from_env.html)- match_ - recognize_ - limit_ - from_ - env
